item.title: Reading Sensors, Reading Docs
item.description: You will probably spend more time figuring out what your sensor is doing than you will spend building with it. That is just how this works. And that is okay. A sensor is more like an instrument than a switch. It has a range, a feel, a set of tendencies. You learn it by practicing with it, listening to it, before you decide what to do with it. Hopefully, this guide can give you some method for doing that. Before you wire anything into TouchDesigner, before you think about what the data will do, find out what it actually is.The fastest way to do this is to print raw values directly from CircuitPython to the REPL/Console.import time # (your sensor setup here) while True: print(sensor.some_value) time.sleep(0.1) Watch the numbers for a minute. Move your hand over the sensor. Get close, then far. Change the lighting. Cover it. Let it sit completely still. Ask yourself: What is the range? What's the lowest value you see? The highest? How fast does it change? Is it noisy (jumping around randomly) or stable? What happens at the edges, when nothing is happening, when something is happening strongly? You cannot make good creative decisions about data you haven't looked at. A value that ranges from 0 to 65535 needs to be handled very differently from one that ranges from 18.0 to 32.0. A noisy signal may need smoothing (maybe) before it can drive something. A slow-moving signal might need amplification. None of this is visible until you look at it raw.There are two ways to find out what values your sensor produces: you can observe it (empirical) and you can look it up (documentation). Do both of these, because they tell you different things.Observing tells you what the sensor does in your specific environment, with your specific setup, under the conditions of your project. This is always the ground truth.The datasheet tells you the theoretical limits of the hardware. The absolute maximum and minimum values the sensor is capable of producing. It also tells you what those values “mean.” What physical quantity they correspond to, and how to convert them to useful units.When they disagree, and sometimes they do, trust what you observe, but use the datasheet to understand why.Once you know your range, one of the most useful habits you can build is normalizing — scaling any sensor value to a 0.0 to 1.0 range before you do anything else with it. It is simpler to work with 0-1 than with, say, 0-4095.# Raw value from sensor raw = sensor.proximity # ranges from 0 to 255 # Normalize to 0.0 – 1.0 normalized = raw / 255.0 Now normalized is 0.0 when nothing is near and 1.0 when something is very close. It doesn't matter what the original range was, everything in 0–1 space speaks the same language.From there, mapping means scaling that 0–1 value to whatever range your output needs:# Map normalized value to a TouchDesigner color parameter (0.0 – 1.0 already) color = normalized # Map to an audio frequency range (200Hz – 2000Hz) frequency = 200 + (normalized * 1800) # Map to a rotation in degrees (0° – 360°) rotation = normalized * 360 The formula for most mappings will follow the same logic:output = output_min + (normalized * (output_max - output_min)) This is where your creative decisions actually live. The sensor doesn't decide what the data means for your work. You do, through the choices you make in mapping.When something isn't working, the instinct is to look at the whole system at once. This almost never helps. Instead, test each link in the chain independently, from the sensor outward.sensor hardware ↓ CircuitPython (reads sensor, formats message) ↓ USB serial (sends text to your computer) ↓ TouchDesigner (receives, parses, maps) Step 0 — Is the sensor on or powered? Is thing on? Are you reading me?Step 1 — Is the sensor being read? Add a print() inside your loop and watch the REPL/Console. If values appear and change when you interact with the sensor, this link is working. If you get an error, it's a wiring or library problem.while True: print(sensor.color_raw) # does this print anything? time.sleep(0.1) Step 2 — Is the serial message formatted correctly? Print the exact string you're building before you send it. Look at it carefully, is it what you expect?msg = f"tcs,{r},{g},{b},{c}\n" print(repr(msg)) # repr() shows you hidden characters like \n serial.write(msg.encode()) Step 3 — Is the software receiving anything? Open the object that imports the data and watch it. You should see raw lines appearing. If you don't, the problem is likely the serial connection. Check the port, check that no other app has the port open.Step 4 — Is the software parsing it correctly? Add a print() inside a DAT Execute script in TD:def onRowChange(dat, rows): for row in rows: line = dat[row, 0].val.strip() print(f"received: {line}") # does this show up in the Textport? parts = line.split(',') print(f"parts: {parts}") # are the parts what you expect? Isolating each step means you always know exactly where the problem is. This is called narrowing the scope.Documentation is a set of answers to questions you haven't asked yet. The skill is knowing which questions to ask and where to look for the answers.For Adafruit sensors, start at the Adafruit product page for your specific sensor — search the sensor name plus "Adafruit." The product page has: A wiring diagram A CircuitPython quickstart guide with working example code Links to the CircuitPython library documentation This is almost always your first stop. Adafruit's documentation is among the best in the hardware world: clear, practical, and written for people learning.For the CircuitPython library API, go to docs.circuitpython.org and search for the library name. This tells you every property and method the library exposes — what you can ask the sensor for, and what type of value you get back.For the sensor hardware itself, search for the sensor part number (e.g., "TCS3430 datasheet") and look for a PDF from the manufacturer. The datasheet is the authoritative source on what the hardware is physically capable of.Datasheets are written for electrical engineers and can be intimidating. Read for what you need, not cover to cover. Look for:Electrical characteristics / specifications table — This usually appears near the front. Look for the operating voltage, current draw, and the output range for each measurement. This tells you what numbers to expect.Measurement description — A section explaining what the sensor is actually measuring. For a color sensor, this tells you whether values are raw counts, lux, or something else, and how to interpret them.I2C address — If you need to put two of the same sensor on the same bus, you'll need to change the address on one of them. The datasheet tells you what addresses are available and how to select them.Application / example circuits — Often near the end. Sometimes useful for wiring reference.The rest you can safely skip until you have a specific question later. Which you will…Find the class for your sensor and look at its properties (the values you can read). For example, the AMG8833 library has a pixels property that returns the 8×8 temperature grid. The docs tell you the return type (list of lists), the units (degrees Celsius), and the range.If a property isn't behaving as expected, check: What type does it return? (integer, float, tuple, list?) What are the units? (counts, lux, Celsius, normalized 0–1?) Does it require anything to be enabled first? Search specifically. "APDS9999 CircuitPython proximity range" will get you further than "APDS9999 not working." The Adafruit forums and the CircuitPython GitHub issues are both indexed by Google and often have exactly the question you're asking.If you find an answer in a forum post or GitHub issue, check the date. CircuitPython libraries update frequently and behavior can change between versions. An old answer might still work, but it might not. Verify against the current docs.The most useful shift in how you approach this work is moving from "how do I make it do what I want" to "what does it want to do, and what can I make of that?"Every sensor has tendencies. The AMG8833's 8×8 resolution means it sees the world in 64 squares — that limiting constraint gives the data a particular character. The TCS3430 responds differently to different light temperatures in ways that are unpredictable until you test them in your actual space.These are the sensor's personality: the particular way it translates the physical world into numbers. Work with that.Print the raw values. Watch them. Find the edges. Then decide what to do.Not all sources are equally useful. When you're troubleshooting, knowing where to look, and how much to trust what you find, saves enormous amounts of time.High trust: Manufacturer documentation and official datasheets The official CircuitPython library documentation (docs.circuitpython.org) Adafruit's product guides and Learning System tutorials The official GitHub repository for any library you're using These sources are authoritative. They describe what the hardware and software actually do. When in doubt, go here first.Medium trust: Stack Overflow answers with significant upvotes and a recent date Adafruit and Arduino forum posts where the original poster confirmed the solution worked GitHub issues where the problem was resolved These are often genuinely useful but require some judgment. Check the date — library behavior changes between versions. Check whether the person asking had the same specific situation you have.Low trust: Random blog posts and tutorials of unknown origin YouTube tutorials without a clear author or source AI-generated answers (including from tools like ChatGPT or Claude) This last point is worth dwelling on. AI tools can be useful for understanding concepts, getting oriented in an unfamiliar area, or generating starting-point code. But they will confidently give you wrong library calls, outdated syntax, and hallucinated function names. Anything an AI tells you about specific code should be verified against the actual documentation before you use it. The documentation is the ground truth. The AI is a starting point.The search itself is a skill. "APDS9999 not working" will get you nowhere. "APDS9999 CircuitPython proximity always returns 0" will get you somewhere. Be specific about the sensor, the platform, the symptom, and the context. The more precisely you can describe what's actually happening, the better your results.

item.title: Learning to Play — On Not Knowing Yet
item.description: When a person sits down at a piano for the first time and plays a wrong note, nothing bad happens. They play it again. They adjust. It is as simple as that. Nobody grades the wrong note. Nobody expects the right one yet; especially not in the very beginning. In fact, the whole situation of learning an instrument, any instrument, is predicated on the idea that you will sound bad before you sound good There is no “problem to solve” here, just a process to move through. The learning happens inside the fumbling, not after it.Experimental media work has the same structure. It just doesn't always feel that way. Especially in an institutional/academic setting.Many students enter technical and creative work carrying an invisible question: am I doing this right? That question is understandable. However, it is also almost always the least useful one to ask yourself. The institutional frame that produces it (grades, evaluation, correct answers) is useful in some contexts and actively counterproductive in most others. When working experimentally, “right” or “correct” is not a fixed target. You're trying to figure out what you are doing, and what comes next.The shift worth making, as early as possible, is to go from performing competence, instead, to practicing curiosity. Performing competence means managing how your work looks to others. Practicing curiosity means following what interests you, especially when you don't know where it leads.A musician learning a new piece doesn't start by playing it through. They start with a single phrase or note. They play it slowly, faster than they can play it correctly, then slowly again. They loop the hard part until it stops being difficult. They listen to what they're producing, not just whether it “matches” the score, but what it actually sounds like, what it feels like, how it sounds in the room. Then they repeat. They make the same mistake many, many, many… many times. Notice the mistake. Then adjust.This is the method.Working with sensors, code, and physical materials asks for the same thing. You don't understand a sensor by reading about it and then deploying it. You understand it by running it, printing its raw values, moving your hand over it, covering it, changing the light, changing its conditions, then watching what changes and what doesn't. You repeat. You adjust. You see (or hear) what it's giving you before you decide what to do with it.The sensor doesn't know your deadline or what grade you “need.” It just responds to the physical world, and your job, right now, is to learn how.In experimental work, trial and error is the primary method.There's a meaningful difference between random trial and error and structured trial and error.Random trial and error: change several things at once, hope something works, have no idea what fixed it or why.Structured trial and error: change one thing, observe what happens, draw a conclusion, repeat. This is slow in the moment and fast overall, because every iteration teaches you something you can use.The habit to build is simple: when something doesn't work, change one thing at a time. Then look at what changed. The goal of each experiment is not to fix the problem. the goal is to learn something specific about the system. The fix will follow the learning.This is also how you build intuition. Intuition is practice: pattern recognition built from many structured observations. The person who "just knows" what's wrong with a circuit or a piece of code got there by breaking things systematically, many times over, and paying attention.Not knowing is the starting condition for all learning. In experimental work it never fully goes away; you just get more comfortable with it.The practitioners you admire, the ones whose work seems fluent and confident, got there by being confused many times and continuing anyway. They built a tolerance for not knowing that eventually started to feel like curiosity. When that happens, confusion becomes interesting rather than threatening.That shift doesn't happen all at once. But it starts with recognizing that what is actually happening here? is usually a more useful question than am I doing this right? One opens things up; the other closes them down.You are learning to play. The wrong notes are part of it.

item.title: Journal Entry 2 — First Impasse Report
item.description:
Due: Before Week 07 Part of: ASN 2: Critical Technical Journal — Installment 2An impasse is a site of inquiry. It is a place where the work has become honest about something it couldn't have told you before you got this far. Your journal entry should reflect that: describe what you're finding, not what went wrong or what you apologize for.Philip Agre called these moments hassles: recurring frictions that keep appearing at the same point in your practice, for reasons that aren't immediately clear. His argument was that hassles are worth studying rather than just fixing, because they reveal the structural gap between how a system models the world and how the world actually works.That gap is valuable information.1. Name the impasse precisely."My sensor isn't working" tells you nothing. Describe exactly what happens, when, under what conditions, and what you expected instead. Be specific enough that someone who hasn't seen your project would understand what you're observing.Vague: "TouchDesigner keeps crashing." Better: "The Serial DAT receives data correctly for about 30 seconds, then stops updating. Reopening the port fixes it temporarily. This happens every time, at roughly the same interval."The act of describing it precisely is itself part of the method. You often begin to find answers in the act of writing the question down clearly.2. What assumption were you making that this disconfirms?Behind every impasse is something you were treating as settled that turns out not to be. It might be an assumption about a tool's capability, a material's behavior, a protocol's reliability, a body's response, or an environment's consistency.Name it directly: I was assuming that ____. This impasse is telling me that isn't true, or isn't reliably true, or is only true under certain conditions.3. Where in your matter-network does the friction live?Your project is a network of relations: sensor, cable, library, code, software, body, environment, all maintained through active labor. The impasse has a location in that network. It lives at a specific connection between specific elements.Try to identify it. Is it a hardware-software boundary? A protocol mismatch? A material behavior the digital system can't represent? A timing issue between two parts of the chain? Being precise about location is being precise about what kind of problem this actually is.4. What becomes possible now that you know this?An impasse is also a decision point. Three directions are usually available: Route around it — redesign your constraints to avoid the friction. This is sometimes the right call, but do it consciously rather than reflexively. Go through it — treat the friction as an enabling constraint. What does the resistance want to do? Can you work with that rather than against it? Let it reframe the project — sometimes an impasse reveals that a core assumption of the project needs to change. This is the most uncomfortable option and often the most generative. Whatever form your journal takes — written, audio, video, annotated screenshots, sketchbook — this entry should be substantial enough to show genuine inquiry, not just observation.The evaluation criteria are depth of engagement and honest tracking of what the friction is revealing.Agre's Critical Technical Practice argues for a split identity in technical work: one foot in the making, one foot in critique of the making. The practitioner who only makes becomes fluent but loses the capacity to see the assumptions they're operating inside of. The critical foot keeps reopening the black boxes that fluency closes.This journal entry is an exercise in that critical foot. The question is what is this telling me about my system, my tools, my assumptions, my project?
Thread: Failure as Method
W05B: First Impasse
Reading Sensors, Reading Docs — if the impasse is technical, the "test the chain one link at a time" section is a useful complement to this entry

item.title: First Impasse
item.description: An impasse is a signal. It reveals something about your project's assumptions that you couldn't have seen before you got here. The First Impasse Report is a site of inquiry.Research-Creation Entanglement Failure as Method Physical-Digital Entanglement Enabling ConstraintsAn impasse is a moment where the project is telling you something about its own structure. It might feel like a malfunction, but it is carrying information.Agre calls these hassles: recurring frictions that keep appearing at the same point in your workflow. They are worth writing down and sitting with before you route around them. What they reveal about the gap between your tool's model of the world and the world itself is often more valuable than any fix.The First Impasse Report asks you to do this formally: describe the problem with enough precision that it becomes a site of inquiry.Address these four things in your journal entry:1. Name the impasse. Describe it precisely. Not "my sensor isn't working" but: what specifically happens, when, under what conditions, and what you expected instead.2. What assumption did you make that this is disconfirming? You were assuming something was settled that isn't. What was it? About your tools, your materials, your process, your project?3. What is it revealing about your matter-network? Which connection in the network is the site of friction? Is it hardware, software, a protocol, a material behavior, a mismatch between two systems?4. What becomes possible now that you know this? An impasse is also a decision point. You can route around it, go through it, or redesign your constraints around it. Which direction does this one want to go?
item.guid: DIGM 553/Week 05 - Enact Thought/submodules/DIGM 553 - W05B - First Impasse.md

item.title: Matter-Networks and Becoming Digital
item.description: Camus & Vinck on digital materiality: digital objects have texture, resistance, and agency. Moving a project into digital form is a transformation. Something is gained and something is lost.Research-Creation Entanglement Failure as Method Physical-Digital Entanglement Enabling ConstraintsBecoming digital. Moving something into a digital system creates a new object with different properties. The original and the digital version have different properties. Something is gained; something is lost. They are two different things.Digital objects have thickness. They break. They resist. They require maintenance. They behave differently across platforms, versions, and conditions. Treating them as transparent or frictionless hides the labor and the loss involved in maintaining that smoothness.Scripts and inscriptions. Every digital tool has a script: embedded assumptions about valid inputs, valid operations, valid outputs. When you use a tool, you partially accept its script. Part of critical technical practice is knowing when you're complying with the script and when you're pushing against it.Matter-network. Your project is a set of relations between things, maintained through active labor. The sensor, the cable, the library, the code, the laptop, the power supply, the body using it: none of these alone is "the project." The project lives in the connections between them. Change any element and you change the network. Where in your project has "becoming digital" created a new object rather than a copy? What did you gain? What is no longer there? What is the script of your primary tool? What does it assume you want to do? Are you working with that assumption or against it? Name every element in your matter-network right now. Which connections are stable? Which are fragile? Where is the maintenance labor concentrated?
item.guid: DIGM 553/Week 05 - Enact Thought/submodules/DIGM 553 - W05A - Matter-Networks and Becoming Digital.md

Three rounds: flat, folded, crumpled.For each state: What does it respond to? What would change it? Then: If this were an instrument, what would it measure or express?We are not warming up. We are practicing the disposition.Scripts + Inscriptions Every tool encodes a theory of use: valid inputs, valid operations, valid outputs. To use a tool is to partially accept its worldview. Critical practice means knowing when you're complying and when you're pushing back.Thickness of Digital Objects Digital objects break, resist, require maintenance, behave differently across versions and environments. The fiction of frictionless digital experience hides enormous labor and loss.Becoming Digital Moving something into a digital system is not copying it, it is creating a new object. Something is gained. Something is irretrievably lost. The two objects are not the same thing in two formats.Unfolding Digital Materiality (Part 2)Failure and impasse are not obstacles to the project. They are data about the project — revealing the formative conditions, hidden assumptions, and structural tensions that define what the work is actually doing.Agre's concept of the hassle is foundational here: not a one-time crash, but a recurring friction — something that keeps happening at the same point in your workflow, for reasons you can't quite name. Hassles are worth writing down. They are the system telling you something structural about the gap between how your tool models the world and how the world actually works.The move Agre names — and this course practices — is to treat impasse as an intellectual resource. When something fails repeatedly, don't just fix it and move on. Ask: what assumption was I making that this failure is disconfirming? What was I treating as settled that isn't? These are the questions the Critical Technical Journal is built to hold.Manning & Massumi's concept of immanent critique is also relevant here: failure, encountered from inside the practice, reveals the pressure points of the system. You can't see those pressure points from outside. You find them by building, hitting walls, and noticing where the resistance is structural rather than incidental.
Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9 What's a recurring friction in your current workflow — not a one-off problem, but something that keeps coming back? What is that hassle about? What assumption does it keep bumping against? When you hit a dead end in a project, how do you usually respond? Do you route around it, sit with it, or abandon it? What would it look like to study it instead? What's the difference between a failure that tells you something and one that doesn't? How do you tell them apart in the moment? If you had to name your most productive creative failure — the one that most changed how you work — what would you call it? What intermediation term would Agre give it?
Agre — *Critical Technical Practice* — the source of the hassle concept and the method of treating recurring friction as intellectual data.
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — immanent critique as the practice of finding pressure points from inside the system.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   Entanglement   Collective PracticeFailure as MethodPhysical and digital aren't two separate domains with an interface between them. They're entangled — each one shaping the other.The signal chain at the center of this course — body → sensor → microcontroller → protocol → software → output — is not a pipeline that converts physical reality into digital representation. It's a series of transformations. At each arrow, something is amplified and something is reduced. The body that touches a capacitive sensor is not the same as the threshold-crossing event the sensor registers. The OSC message is not the gesture. Something is always gained; something is always lost. The question is whether you know which — and whether that choice is deliberate.Magnusson puts it directly: the digital system is "material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." All three layers are active at once. The hardware has physical affordances that shape where you can put it and what it can touch. The firmware has timing properties that shape resolution and latency. The software has representational assumptions that shape what the data means. None of these layers is neutral; together they constitute the instrument.This thread tracks how physical and digital forces meet, condition each other, and produce something neither could alone — across hardware choices, material selections, installation environments, and bodies moving through space.
Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9, Week 10 At each arrow in your signal chain, what's being amplified and what's being reduced? Is that tradeoff intentional? What does your system not know about the body it's sensing — and what can happen in that gap? Where does the physical environment shape the digital behavior, and vice versa? Can you design the entanglement rather than just inheriting it? What material are your sensors touching? What cultural or social charge does that material carry — and does your system acknowledge it?
Magnusson — *Epistemic Tools* — on instruments as material-electric-symbolic systems.
Camus + Vinck — *Unfolding Digital Materiality* — on the thickness and materiality of digital objects.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   EntanglementPhysical-Digital EntanglementA constraint that opens things up rather than just closing them down.Manning & Massumi's example: gravity. You can't dance without gravity — remove it and there's no jump, no landing, no arc. Gravity is implacable, but it's also what makes the jump possible. Add horizontal momentum and "the arc of the jump will be a collaboration between the action of gravity and the energy and angular momentum of the horizontal movement acting as co-causes." That's an enabling constraint in action — resistance that generates something rather than just blocking it.The key distinction is between limitative constraints (dead ends) and enabling ones (co-causes). A limitative constraint just says stop. An enabling constraint pushes back in a way that makes something happen that wouldn't otherwise. The trick is figuring out which you're dealing with — and sometimes, how to convert one into the other.This shows up everywhere in the course. The MPR121 has 12 channels — that's a constraint, but it's also the specific sculptural logic of the thing. OSC over UDP drops packets — that's a constraint, but it forces real-time compositional decisions you wouldn't otherwise have to make. The 3-hour session is a constraint; it's also what allows the kind of depth you can't get in 50 minutes.
Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 8 What's the gravity in your practice — the resistance you can't remove? Is it enabling or just limitative? What would it take to convert it? What's the difference between a constraint someone handed you and one you designed yourself? When you hit a wall, is it a dead end or a co-cause waiting to be found? What if you designed your constraints before you designed the content?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — Propositions 0–3.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Entanglement   Failure as Method   Physical-Digital EntanglementEnabling ConstraintsPractitioner, tool, and material do not interact as pre-formed, separate entities. They are mutually constituted through the practice itself. You don't bring a self to a tool — the self that acts is partly made by the act.Barad's posthumanist performativity replaces interaction (between pre-existing things) with intra-action (the process through which distinct agencies emerge). An apparatus — for Barad, any material-discursive arrangement that makes knowledge possible — doesn't just measure or represent phenomena; it participates in producing them. The researcher, the instrument, and the phenomenon are all co-constituted through the apparatus.For this course, that means: you are not a stable subject using a neutral tool to study an external object. You are entangled with your hardware, your software, your materials, and the site of your practice. These entanglements are not metaphors — they are structural features of how knowledge gets made. Documenting them honestly is part of what the Critical Technical Journal is for.Camus & Vinck extend this into digital materiality: the digital is not immaterial. It is made of matter — servers, cables, electricity, screen light. Every "digital" thing has a thickness, a weight, a set of dependencies. The click is a material event. The file is an inscription on physical media. Recognizing this thickness is how you stop treating your tools as transparent windows onto some other reality.
Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9 What are you entangled with in your current project — not just using, but mutually constituted by? What would change about the project if that entanglement changed? Barad replaces "interaction" with "intra-action." What's the difference? Try to locate an intra-action — a moment where the boundaries between you, your tool, and your material were genuinely unclear. Where does the "digital" in your practice have material weight — consume power, require infrastructure, produce heat, leave traces? If your apparatus (the whole material-discursive arrangement of your practice) is not just measuring phenomena but helping produce them — what phenomena is yours producing?
Camus + Vinck — *Unfolding Digital Materiality* — on the thickness of digital objects; the materiality of inscription and infrastructure.
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — the concept of co-causality and conditioning is entanglement in practice.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   Physical-Digital Entanglement   Failure as MethodEntanglementMaking and thinking as the same act — not phases, not sequence, not illustration.The standard model: you research something, then you make something that shows what you found. Research-creation refuses that split. Manning & Massumi locate it at what they call the prebifurcation point — the moment before making and thinking get separated into different institutional categories with different evaluation criteria. At that point, making is thinking, and thinking is already a practice.The thing this rules out is the communication model — the idea that your creative work is "delivering" research results you already had. If the project knows its outcome before it starts, it's not research-creation. The work has to be genuinely open to something it couldn't have predicted.What that actually requires in practice: conditioning rather than framing. Framing means you set up a structure and the work fills it in. Conditioning means you bring things into contact — materials, tools, questions, bodies, sensors — and stay open to what emerges from their interaction. Neither you nor any individual element fully determines the outcome.For this course: the journal is not documentation of a separate making process. The making is not an illustration of the thinking. They interpenetrate, or it's not research-creation.
Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9, Week 10, Week 11 Where in your workflow do making and thinking actually happen at the same time? Can you work from that moment deliberately? Is your project conditioned or framed? What are you holding open, and what are you predetermining? If your practice is already "thinking something" — what is it thinking right now? What in your institution (program, discipline, grading rubric) separates your thinking from your making? How do you work inside that without just reproducing it?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — Propositions 0–3.
Loveless — *Haraway's Dog* — on curiosity as a research method; following a question rather than testing a hypothesis.
Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   Entanglement   Failure as Method   Making PublicResearch-Creation

item.title: Week 04
item.description:
making is knowingdigital has weightno view from nowheretool has a scriptHaraway's DogUnfolding Digital MaterialityThe Dog Your entry point into research is much more a relation than it is any specific topic. The specific, non-generalizable tangle of curiosity, body, and material that you choose to follow. Research begins with a commitment. And that commitment leads immediately to question(s).Situated Knowledge Haraway: there is no view from nowhere. All knowledge is partial, located, embodied. The fiction of objectivity is a way of hiding whose body is doing the knowing.Research-Creation Loveless extends this into practice: the work you make is not separate from the knowing. Making is the method. The dog is what keeps you honest about what you are actually inside of.Digital as Material Digital objects are not immaterial. Code, data, and interfaces have weight — they break down, resist, accumulate friction. Camus + Vinck insist on treating digital things as things, with their own agencies and constraints.Scripts and Prescriptions Every digital tool has a script — a built-in theory of use. The tool prescribes what counts as valid input, valid action, valid output. To use the tool is to partially accept its script.Material-Digital Entanglement The digital does not float above the physical — it is entangled with it. Hardware, software, bodies, and environments co-constitute what the system can and cannot do.What is the relation — not the topic — that you are already committed to? What keeps pulling you back before you even have a research question?Where in your signal chain does a tool's script conflict with what your material is actually doing? What gets lost in that translation?Is your knowledge claim about the material, or about what happens to the material when your apparatus touches it? Can you tell the difference?What is one thing your tools assume that you have stopped questioning? How does that assumption shape what your project can become?Whose body was imagined when your primary tool was designed? Are you working inside that imagination or against it?You are not starting from zero. You have a body, a history, a set of tools, and a relation you keep returning to. The proposal is meant to be a a plan for what you will do. It is meant to be the constraints you setup in order to practice within and make artifacts.Name it. Commit to it. Design from there.Enabling constraints as situated commitments. A constraint is not a limitation you impose from outside. It is an honest acknowledgment of what you are already inside.Both texts agree on specificity. Loveless: the dog cannot be generalized. Camus + Vinck: the digital thing cannot be abstracted from its material conditions. You cannot research, make, or build in general.The script is part of the dog. If your entry point is a material process, the tools you use to sense and process it are participants in that observation. They have prior understanding. They have scripts. In this way, your dog is already entangled with them.What is your dog? Loveless, Haraway, and the specificity of situated knowledge. Proposal workshopping.Loveless's reading of Haraway: 'your dog' is your specific, situated, non-generalizable entry point into research. It is not a topic but a relation — the particular tangle of curiosity, material, and context that only you can follow.Research-Creation Enabling Constraints EntanglementLoveless gives us the "dog" as a figure for situated, non-generalizable knowledge. You cannot research in general. You research from somewhere specific — a body, a relation, a material entanglement you are already inside of. Haraway's original move was to say that the dog is not a metaphor for the researcher; it is the actual site of inquiry. The specificity is the method.Camus & Vinck (Part 1) extend this into practice: tools and materials are not neutral instruments that you pick up and put down. They have histories, they encode assumptions, they shape what you can notice and what you cannot. Working with a tool is working inside a worldview.The two readings together ask the same question from different angles: What have you already committed to, and do you know it?That is what the proposal is trying to surface — not a plan, but an honest account of your situated starting point.DIGM 553 - W04A - What Is Your DogProject Title: Did Sun Ra Fear Cryosleep? Researcher: Darren Woodland, Jr. Course: DIGM 553/753My entry point is dissolution. A commitment to the entanglement of materiality and time. Specifically, the acoustic behavior of materials as they break down in water; and what it might mean to listen to that process as composition. A metaphor for the bodies, souls, and memories of those lost in Atlantic Slave Trade. Dissolved and deposited by the salt of the ocean. The question I keep returning to is not what does this sound like but what does this process already know? Substrate dissolution is a form of material memory. The hydrophone doesn't record it so much as it makes it legible through is very specific observational form.The title of this work, Did Sun Ra Fear Cryosleep?, holds the tension I am working in: between preservation and release, between a body suspended in wait and a body that has already gone. Sun Ra's cosmological thinking was often about escape. Escape from category, from Earth, from the conditions that confined Black life in his time (and now). Cryosleep is a fantasy, or perhaps a fallacy, of control over that escape. A means to explore the tensions of modern western sci-fi depictions of “colonial/colony ships” and the bodies suspended in transport aboard them; traversing space-time to “escape.” In a way dissolution being listened to is a refusal of control. It goes on its own terms and is the generative material for processes with just as much lack of control.This is my dog: the specific, non-transferable relation between listening, material change, and what Black cosmological thought does to the idea of escape, preservation, and control.Materials: water, soluble substrate — salt, chalk, sugar each dissolve differently — turbidity/temperature/TDS sensors, hydrophone, Zoom H5, laptop, speaker array.Environment: The dissolution happens in a contained vessel. The sensors report its state; the hydrophone listens from inside it. The speakers extend the process into the room. The listener hears a composed version of something that is also actually happening in real-time.Three constraints that shape the work without predetermining it:1. The sensor network monitors, not interprets. (Material Constraint) Turbidity, temperature, and TDS sensors track the dissolution state of the substrate continuously. The hydrophone — itself piezoelectric, meaning it listens through contact with the medium — captures the acoustic behavior of that same process. The constraint is that no single sensor speaks for the whole.2. Minimal but honest processing of the raw capture. (Technical Constraint) The Zoom H5 transmits (not records) what the hydrophone picks up. That signal passes through EQ before entering Max/MSP in an attempt to make it legible to DataKnot and Somax2. The EQ is a translation layer. The constraint is that processing stops where interpretation begins.3. The AI listens before I do. (Affective Constraint) Somax2 ingests the live hydrophone signal and generates its response before anyone hears a playback mix. My role is to curate the output, not author it. This keeps the agency distributed across material, algorithm, and body.Max/MSP is not a neutral tool. It encodes a particular logic of signal flow. A logic of discrete objects, patch cables, top-to-bottom data movement. This logic comes out of mid-century electronic music and telecommunications research. It assumes modularity. It assumes you can isolate a process, route it, transform it, and route it again without the transformation changing the thing, fundamentally, without intent.I am working with and against that assumption. The dissolution I am listening to is not modular. It does not isolate cleanly. Somax2 adds another layer: it is trained on corpora, it has priors, it responds to pattern. It is not listening the way I listen or the way the water listens. That difference is generative. I am not trying to make the system simulate the material, what I am trying to do is make those incommensurable modes of listening produce something together that none of them could produce alone.The broader epistemic question the work is asking: what does it mean to let a material process be a composer? And what does it mean to build a system that is honest about the fact that it cannot fully hear what it is working with, unlike a composer?The department needs to see a project that demonstrates technical rigor and conceptual coherence; a clear connection between the readings and the making decisions, and evidence that I understand what an enabling constraint actually does. The course context also needs something that can be assessed: a legible document, a traceable methodology, an artifact that can be presented and discussed.What my practice needs is different. Did Sun Ra Fear Cryosleep? is not primarily a demonstration of technical competence. It is an attempt to listen to a material process that has already decided what it is going to do, and to build a system honest enough to admit it cannot fully hear or control that. The work is successful, from inside my practice, if it stays uncomfortable and uncontrollable.The gap: the course needs completion and legibility. My practice needs the work to remain open and a little unresolved. These are not irreconcilable, but they pull in different directions. The proposal format itself is a boundary object, it asks me to be precise about something that is still becoming. I am writing it knowing that the project will outgrow whatever I say here, and that is fine too.This is a living document. The proposal will be revised in Week 10 to reflect what the project has become.Speculative Proposal — ExampleYour Proposal is a Story Not a plan, a story. A story about what you are already committed to and why that commitment matters. Your methods help tell that story. Barad asks us to reconsider a pretty basic assumption: that things exist before their relations. i.e.: That you are one thing, Your tool is another thing, and Your material is yet another thing And then those things interact. They say no. The boundaries between things are not given. They are enacted through practice and relation. This is what is meant by intra-action rather than interaction.Interaction assumes two pre-formed entities coming together: you + Touchdesigner (TD), each fully formed, exchanging influence.Intra-action says: the entities emerge through the relation. The version of you that exists when you're deep in a patchwork is not the same version of you that existed before. The version of TD that exists in your practice is not the same as TD in the abstract. The practice/relation constitutes both.Barad uses the word apparatus for the whole material-discursive arrangement through which knowledge gets made. An apparatus includes the social, institutional, and conceptual structures that make a particular kind of inquiry possible (through the faculties of the object). The lab, the protocol, the grant structure, the assumptions of the field, all apparatus.For this course: your apparatus includes your hardware, your software, your studio space, your practice context, the course itself, the readings, your collaborators. That is because they are all co-constituting the phenomena you're making.
Bluecadet builds for institutions: museums, cultural centers, public spaces. Their work is entangled with architecture, with curators, with conservation concerns, with visitor behavior at scales from one person to thousands. The "tool" is never just software; it's a whole apparatus including the wall it is mounted on and the demographic of who walks past it.
Meow Wolf is an interesting case: they're a collective that became a company. Something changed in the apparatus. The entanglements shifted: new stakeholders, new financial structures, new obligations. What did that do to what was possible to make? This is Barad's point made very concrete.
BRDG studios works with clients communities where the entanglement is highly relational. The apparatus includes trust. It includes narrative and creative vision. It includes whether people in that room feel the purpose and story by what was built. That's its in the apparatus.If you are entangled with your tools, mutually constituted by them, then the tool audit is a map of the conditions of your own practice. You're not standing outside your tools observing them. You're in it. The audit is a way of trying to see something you're inside of.That's hard. It is supposed to be hard.
Epistemic Tools Entanglement Research-Creation Physical-Digital EntanglementBarad, K. (2007). Meeting the Universe Halfway: Quantum Physics and the Entanglement of Matter and Meaning. Duke University Press.DIGM 553 - W03C - Barad — Entanglement and Intra-actionYour signal chain is a matter network None of its parts are the "thing." The thing is the set of associations between them, maintained through active labor. The project is its network of relations. Understanding it means following what it connects, not reducing it to what it "is." You can consider this proposal as a form of “ethics document,” to echo Loveless. When designing enabling constraints, you are making a claim about what you are willing to foreclose, about the trust around your material/object, and how you are positioning yourself within the research.The Boundary Object The boundary object gives you the permission to stop trying to force your work fit cleanly into one category/silo. The project that embraces the “boundary object,” can speak to multiple communities (the department, the field, the art world, a grant committee, a future employer, etc.). Giving it much more circulation potential and more staying power. Agential cut (Barad) is the most fundamental unit: every act of measurement, sensing, or processing enacts a boundary. The CUT produces from a specific context.Boundary work (Camus + Vinck) is what agential cuts look like in practice, at the level of technical labor. It's the ongoing, contested, material effort to stabilize an agential cut.Boundary object (Bowker + Star via Loveless) operates at the social/institutional scale. Once the cuts have been made and the boundaries have been worked, the resulting artifact circulates across communities that care about different things.StabilizationProductionCirculationUnsettlingRemixingEmbodyingTransmittingof 4Speculative Proposal — ExampleSpeculative Proposal — ExampleProject Title: Did Sun Ra Fear Cryosleep?Researcher: Darren Woodland, Jr.Course: DIGM 553/753(a) Driving Curiosity → “What Is Your Dog?”My entry point is dissolution. A commitment to the entanglement of materi-ality and time. Specifically, the acoustic behavior of materials as they breakdown in water; and what it might mean to listen to that process as composition.A metaphor for the bodies, souls, and memories of those lost in Atlantic SlaveTrade. Dissolved and deposited by the salt of the ocean. The question I keepreturning to is not what does this sound like but what does this process alreadyknow? Substrate dissolution is a form of material memory. The hydrophonedoesn't record it so much as it makes it legible through is very specific observa-tional form.The title of this work, Did Sun Ra Fear Cryosleep?, holds the tension I amworking in: between preservation and release, between a body suspended inwait and a body that has already gone. Sun Ra's cosmological thinking wasoften about escape. Escape from category, from Earth, from the conditions thatconfined Black life in his time (and now). Cryosleep is a fantasy, or perhaps afallacy, of control over that escape. A means to explore the tensions of modernwestern sci-fi depictions of “colonial/colony ships” and the bodies suspended intransport aboard them; traversing space-time to “escape.” In a way dissolutionbeing listened to is a refusal of control. It goes on its own terms and is thegenerative material for processes with just as much lack of control.This is my dog: the specific, non-transferable relation between listen-ing, material change, and what Black cosmological thought does tothe idea of escape, preservation, and control.1(b) Matter-Network — Signal Chain
2
Speculative Proposal — Example1Speculative Proposal — Example.pdfThe crafting of a research question is the crafting of a story that is also the crafting of an ethics.Is Music theory a description of what you are doing or is it a prescription for what you should do?Languages (discourses) precede us; research methods and disciplines precede us. We enter into them and they work to craft the possible forms of our questions. Thus, when examining our research practices, it is crucial to ask: which stories are animating our choices? Why might this research choice matter? Alternate (research) stories create alternate (research) worlds. Conversely, different storytelling strategies (methods and practices) emerge from different worldviews and commitments. Peer workshopping of the Speculative Proposal. The proposal articulates: (a) your driving curiosity; (b) selected enabling constraints; (c) the matter-network of tools/materials; (d) your Epistemic Positioning Statement ; (e) your Boundary Object.
Research-Creation Enabling Constraints Entanglement~10 minutes. Individual, then brief share-out.
Read the Example Speculative Proposal (Did Sun Ra Fear Cryosleep?).Write your answers to these three questions about your own project: What is your dog? — Not your topic. Your specific entry point. The thing you want to follow, determined by your curiosity and experience. What is your signal chain? — List your materials, tools, and environments in order. What is the first thing? What is the last? What happens in between? What does your main tool assume? — Pick one tool you are using (software, hardware, environment). What worldview is baked into it? Are you working with that or against it?
See: Speculative Proposal — Example (Did Sun Ra Fear Cryosleep?)DIGM 553 - W04B - Speculative Proposal Workshop

item.title: Research-Creation
item.description:
Making and thinking as the same act — not phases, not sequence, not illustration.The standard model: you research something, then you make something that shows what you found. Research-creation refuses that split. Manning & Massumi locate it at what they call the prebifurcation point — the moment before making and thinking get separated into different institutional categories with different evaluation criteria. At that point, making is thinking, and thinking is already a practice.The thing this rules out is the communication model — the idea that your creative work is "delivering" research results you already had. If the project knows its outcome before it starts, it's not research-creation. The work has to be genuinely open to something it couldn't have predicted.What that actually requires in practice: conditioning rather than framing. Framing means you set up a structure and the work fills it in. Conditioning means you bring things into contact — materials, tools, questions, bodies, sensors — and stay open to what emerges from their interaction. Neither you nor any individual element fully determines the outcome.For this course: the journal is not documentation of a separate making process. The making is not an illustration of the thinking. They interpenetrate, or it's not research-creation.Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9, Week 10, Week 11 Where in your workflow do making and thinking actually happen at the same time? Can you work from that moment deliberately? Is your project conditioned or framed? What are you holding open, and what are you predetermining? If your practice is already "thinking something" — what is it thinking right now? What in your institution (program, discipline, grading rubric) separates your thinking from your making? How do you work inside that without just reproducing it?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — Propositions 0–3.
Loveless — *Haraway's Dog* — on curiosity as a research method; following a question rather than testing a hypothesis.
Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   Entanglement   Failure as Method   Making Public

item.title: Failure as Method
item.description:
Failure and impasse are not obstacles to the project. They are data about the project — revealing the formative conditions, hidden assumptions, and structural tensions that define what the work is actually doing.Agre's concept of the hassle is foundational here: not a one-time crash, but a recurring friction — something that keeps happening at the same point in your workflow, for reasons you can't quite name. Hassles are worth writing down. They are the system telling you something structural about the gap between how your tool models the world and how the world actually works.The move Agre names — and this course practices — is to treat impasse as an intellectual resource. When something fails repeatedly, don't just fix it and move on. Ask: what assumption was I making that this failure is disconfirming? What was I treating as settled that isn't? These are the questions the Critical Technical Journal is built to hold.Manning & Massumi's concept of immanent critique is also relevant here: failure, encountered from inside the practice, reveals the pressure points of the system. You can't see those pressure points from outside. You find them by building, hitting walls, and noticing where the resistance is structural rather than incidental.Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9 What's a recurring friction in your current workflow — not a one-off problem, but something that keeps coming back? What is that hassle about? What assumption does it keep bumping against? When you hit a dead end in a project, how do you usually respond? Do you route around it, sit with it, or abandon it? What would it look like to study it instead? What's the difference between a failure that tells you something and one that doesn't? How do you tell them apart in the moment? If you had to name your most productive creative failure — the one that most changed how you work — what would you call it? What intermediation term would Agre give it?
Agre — *Critical Technical Practice* — the source of the hassle concept and the method of treating recurring friction as intellectual data.
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — immanent critique as the practice of finding pressure points from inside the system.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   Entanglement   Collective Practice

item.title: Entanglement
item.description:
Practitioner, tool, and material do not interact as pre-formed, separate entities. They are mutually constituted through the practice itself. You don't bring a self to a tool — the self that acts is partly made by the act.Barad's posthumanist performativity replaces interaction (between pre-existing things) with intra-action (the process through which distinct agencies emerge). An apparatus — for Barad, any material-discursive arrangement that makes knowledge possible — doesn't just measure or represent phenomena; it participates in producing them. The researcher, the instrument, and the phenomenon are all co-constituted through the apparatus.For this course, that means: you are not a stable subject using a neutral tool to study an external object. You are entangled with your hardware, your software, your materials, and the site of your practice. These entanglements are not metaphors — they are structural features of how knowledge gets made. Documenting them honestly is part of what the Critical Technical Journal is for.Camus & Vinck extend this into digital materiality: the digital is not immaterial. It is made of matter — servers, cables, electricity, screen light. Every "digital" thing has a thickness, a weight, a set of dependencies. The click is a material event. The file is an inscription on physical media. Recognizing this thickness is how you stop treating your tools as transparent windows onto some other reality.Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9 What are you entangled with in your current project — not just using, but mutually constituted by? What would change about the project if that entanglement changed? Barad replaces "interaction" with "intra-action." What's the difference? Try to locate an intra-action — a moment where the boundaries between you, your tool, and your material were genuinely unclear. Where does the "digital" in your practice have material weight — consume power, require infrastructure, produce heat, leave traces? If your apparatus (the whole material-discursive arrangement of your practice) is not just measuring phenomena but helping produce them — what phenomena is yours producing?
Camus + Vinck — *Unfolding Digital Materiality* — on the thickness of digital objects; the materiality of inscription and infrastructure.
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — the concept of co-causality and conditioning is entanglement in practice.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   Physical-Digital Entanglement   Failure as Method

item.title: Enabling Constraints
item.description:
A constraint that opens things up rather than just closing them down.Manning & Massumi's example: gravity. You can't dance without gravity — remove it and there's no jump, no landing, no arc. Gravity is implacable, but it's also what makes the jump possible. Add horizontal momentum and "the arc of the jump will be a collaboration between the action of gravity and the energy and angular momentum of the horizontal movement acting as co-causes." That's an enabling constraint in action — resistance that generates something rather than just blocking it.The key distinction is between limitative constraints (dead ends) and enabling ones (co-causes). A limitative constraint just says stop. An enabling constraint pushes back in a way that makes something happen that wouldn't otherwise. The trick is figuring out which you're dealing with — and sometimes, how to convert one into the other.This shows up everywhere in the course. The MPR121 has 12 channels — that's a constraint, but it's also the specific sculptural logic of the thing. OSC over UDP drops packets — that's a constraint, but it forces real-time compositional decisions you wouldn't otherwise have to make. The 3-hour session is a constraint; it's also what allows the kind of depth you can't get in 50 minutes.Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 8 What's the gravity in your practice — the resistance you can't remove? Is it enabling or just limitative? What would it take to convert it? What's the difference between a constraint someone handed you and one you designed yourself? When you hit a wall, is it a dead end or a co-cause waiting to be found? What if you designed your constraints before you designed the content?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — Propositions 0–3.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Entanglement   Failure as Method   Physical-Digital Entanglement

item.title: Collective Practice
item.description:
The studio is not a bunch of individual practices running in parallel. It's a site where practitioners condition each other.Manning & Massumi describe the seminar or studio as an experiment: "For an 'event' to be an event, it is necessary that a collective thinking process be enacted that can give rise to new thoughts through the interaction on site." The key condition: what happens can't be predetermined. If the instructor already knows what conclusions are going to be reached and is just delivering them — that's not an event in this sense.The critique is the most direct version of this. In this course, critique is not judgment. It's activation — attending to someone else's work closely enough to surface what it's doing that it might not know it's doing. A good critique question doesn't say "this works / this doesn't." It opens something: what is this committed to? What does it refuse? What would happen if you followed that refusal further?There's an ethic here too. What you bring to the room — your presence, attention, honest response — is a contribution to a shared environment, not optional. This is part of how the work actually gets made.Week 2, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9, Week 11 What's the difference between a critique that evaluates and one that activates? What does an activating question actually sound like? What do you bring to the room that no one else does? What does the group gain from your specific presence? When you encounter someone else's work, what's your first instinct — assess it, identify with it, question it? What would it mean to just attend to it first? How does your practice change when it's in dialogue? What has a peer's question ever revealed to you about your own work?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — on the studio event and techniques of relation.
Research-Creation   Making Public   Failure as Method   Entanglement

item.title: Physical-Digital Entanglement
item.description:
Physical and digital aren't two separate domains with an interface between them. They're entangled — each one shaping the other.The signal chain at the center of this course — body → sensor → microcontroller → protocol → software → output — is not a pipeline that converts physical reality into digital representation. It's a series of transformations. At each arrow, something is amplified and something is reduced. The body that touches a capacitive sensor is not the same as the threshold-crossing event the sensor registers. The OSC message is not the gesture. Something is always gained; something is always lost. The question is whether you know which — and whether that choice is deliberate.Magnusson puts it directly: the digital system is "material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." All three layers are active at once. The hardware has physical affordances that shape where you can put it and what it can touch. The firmware has timing properties that shape resolution and latency. The software has representational assumptions that shape what the data means. None of these layers is neutral; together they constitute the instrument.This thread tracks how physical and digital forces meet, condition each other, and produce something neither could alone — across hardware choices, material selections, installation environments, and bodies moving through space.Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9, Week 10 At each arrow in your signal chain, what's being amplified and what's being reduced? Is that tradeoff intentional? What does your system not know about the body it's sensing — and what can happen in that gap? Where does the physical environment shape the digital behavior, and vice versa? Can you design the entanglement rather than just inheriting it? What material are your sensors touching? What cultural or social charge does that material carry — and does your system acknowledge it?
Magnusson — *Epistemic Tools* — on instruments as material-electric-symbolic systems.
Camus + Vinck — *Unfolding Digital Materiality* — on the thickness and materiality of digital objects.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   Entanglement

item.title: Epistemic Tools
item.description:
Tools are not neutral. Every instrument encodes a worldview — a set of propositions about what the world is, what can be known about it, and who that knowledge is for.Magnusson, drawing on Hankins & Silverman and Don Ihde, argues that instruments don't merely follow theory — they often determine it, because "instruments determine what is possible, and what is possible determines to a large extent what can be thought." An epistemic tool is any instrument understood this way: as a knowledge-making artifact with its own claims built in.Ihde identifies three modalities of how instruments mediate between body and world: embodiment relations (you act through the tool, which recedes), hermeneutic relations (the tool produces data you must interpret), and alterity relations (you engage with the tool as a quasi-other). These aren't fixed categories — any practice oscillates between them, and the shift matters.Every tool also performs an amplification-reduction: it amplifies certain features of the world and systematically reduces others. The danger isn't reduction itself — all tools must reduce. The danger is when the reduction becomes invisible, when it gets naturalized into what Latour calls a black box: an object whose internal contingency has disappeared through repeated use. Fluency closes black boxes. The critique foot of Agre's split identity keeps reopening them.Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5 What does your primary tool amplify — what becomes easy, visible, measurable? And what does it reduce — what disappears, gets rounded off, or can't be represented? Who designed the defaults in your software? What assumptions about bodies, practices, and contexts are baked into those choices? Which of Ihde's three modalities describes your relationship to your tool right now? When does it shift — and what triggers the shift? What's the most naturalized tool in your practice — the one you've stopped questioning? What would happen if you opened that black box?
Magnusson — *Epistemic Tools* — the source text for the concept; covers Ihde's modalities, amplification-reduction, and the techne/episteme distinction.
Agre — *Critical Technical Practice* — on computational imperialism, the split identity, and the practice of making the invisible assumptions of tools visible.
Research-Creation   Enabling Constraints   Entanglement   Physical-Digital Entanglement   Failure as Method

item.title: Making Public
item.description:
Rendering work public is not the delivery of results. It is a continuation of the research — a way of making the formative conditions and processual transformation of the work available for encounter.Loveless, working through Haraway, argues that research-creation carries an obligation to render research public — not as a finished product submitted to evaluation, but as a practice in itself. What gets made public is not just the artifact but the forces that formed it: the impasses, the enabling constraints, the entanglements, the tools and their reductions. This is why the Final Presentation in this course is not a showcase. It is a rendering.The distinction Loveless makes is between transparency (showing your work) and accountability (taking responsibility for what your work does in the world — including what it can't do, what it excludes, and who it speaks to or past). Accountability requires knowing the stakes of the work, not just the process.For experimental media practice, making public also means confronting the question of audience: who is this for? What does it ask of the people who encounter it? A TouchDesigner patch sent to a hard drive is not public; the same patch running in a gallery space with bodies moving through it is. The difference is not technical. It is relational — and designing that relation is itself a creative and ethical act.Week 6, Week 9, Week 11 What would it mean to make your process public — not just your result? What would you have to show that you've been hiding? Who is the audience for your work, and what does it ask of them? Have you designed that ask, or inherited it from the format? Loveless distinguishes transparency from accountability. Where in your practice are you being transparent (showing your method) without being accountable (owning what the work does or fails to do)? What form is your work made public in, and what does that form assume about who can access it?
Loveless — *Haraway's Dog* — on the obligation to render research public, curiosity as method, and the boundary object.
Research-Creation   Collective Practice   Failure as Method   Entanglement

item.title: Conceptual Threads — DIGM 553
item.description: These eight threads run across all 11 weeks. They are not topics that appear once and disappear — they are recurring structures that deepen each time they're encountered in a new context. Each one is a lens you can hold up to your project at any point in the semester. "The point is not to know in advance where you will arrive, but to follow the thread." Making and thinking are not sequential — they are co-constitutive. Research-creation names the activity at the prebifurcation point, before inquiry and practice diverge into separate institutional logics. The methodology running beneath everything else in this course.Every tool encodes a worldview. When you pick up an instrument, you adopt a set of propositions about what the world is and what can be known about it. This thread asks: what does your tool claim — and are you making that claim consciously?A limitation that generates emergence rather than just restriction. Gravity enables the jump. The 12-point sensor grid enables a particular kind of sculptural thinking. This thread asks: what is the co-cause you're pushing against, and is it working for you?Practitioner, tool, and material are not separate entities that interact. They are mutually constituted through intra-action — through the practice itself. Barad and Camus & Vinck give this claim its theoretical and material grounding.Failure and impasse are data, not obstacles. Agre's concept of the hassle — the recurring friction that reveals structural assumptions — is the engine of the Critical Technical Journal. This thread tracks how your dead ends become your research findings.The signal chain running from body to sensor to microcontroller to software to output is a series of transformations, not a transparent pipeline. This thread follows what is amplified and reduced at each step — and asks what creative work happens in those gaps.Rendering work public is a practice, not a delivery. Loveless and Haraway: research-creation carries an obligation to make formative conditions visible, not just results. This thread tracks how your work encounters audiences and what it asks of them.The studio is a site of collective becoming. Critique is activation, not judgment. Manning & Massumi: the seminar event works when the potential of what might occur isn't pre-reduced to conclusions already reached. This thread tracks how individual practices meet and change each other.

item.title: Speculative Proposal — Template + Guide
item.description:
ASN 1 Component — Due: beginning of Week 5 See full assignment brief: ASN 1: Potluck + Speculative ProposalA proposal in this experimental media arts lab is not meant to be seen as a list of promised deliverables. It is more so a construction of conditions. You are aiming to act with precision (pragmatism) to catalyze the unknown (speculative). Manning and Massumi call this speculative pragmatism: the work of building a situation that allows something not yet known to happen. This document is a living artifact. It will be revised (due at Week 10). The gap between the two versions (what changed and why) is itself part of the research/processes.A PDF to Blackboard. Prose, annotated diagrams, hybrid, etc. If you wish to depart significantly from this structure, talk to me first.What is the specific, situated thing that's pulling you? A relation. A question that has you in it. Loveless, following Haraway, calls this your "dog," the particular thing you can't stop following, the pull that refuses to generalize away. Focus not on what you're making but on whom and what you are touching when you engage this process.Be specific. "I'm interested in how capacitive touch changes when the conductive surface is hair, not metal; what shifts about agency, contact, and consent" is a driving curiosity. "I'm interested in interactivity and the body" is not. Try writing: "I am obsessively inquiring into the gap between and because... What I don't understand yet is..." A map — visual or written — of the tools, materials, environments, bodies, and relations that constitute your project's technical and social apparatus. Not a list, A map. One that shows how things depend on, condition, or transform each other.Pull from your Tool Audit findings here. Locate the specific "theoretical instruments" (the audio buffers, touch thresholds, protocol choices) you're choosing to keep in your loop and why.Include: Hardware and software tools Physical materials, objects, surfaces, spaces Bodies (whose? doing what?) Data (what kind, how captured, how stored) Site or environment Protocols and signal flows Dependencies — what does X require Y for? Unknowns — things you still need to figure out A rough sketch is fine. The point is to see the whole apparatus.Define 3–5 specific, formal rules that will govern your making process. Remember: a constraint is not a limitation; it is a catalyst for surprise. They are conditions that creates productive friction without predetermining the outcome. Constraints should be typed (as in categorized). Aim for at least one of each: Technical constraint — governs your signal chain or tools (e.g., "No audio playback over 1.5 seconds.") Material constraint — governs physical or environmental conditions (e.g., "Must be triggered by physical proximity only — no keyboard/mouse input.") Affective constraint — governs relationship, attention, or intent (e.g., "Incorporate one error from the console as an intentional feature rather than a bug to fix.") For each constraint, write: The constraint: what it is, exactly Why this one: what pressure or generativity you expect from it What it forecloses: what you're giving up (a constraint that forecloses nothing isn't a constraint) Ask yourself: are your constraints based on your skills, or are they hiding your skills? Both are valid starting points, but know which one you're doing.A paragraph (or two) on the epistemics of your project. This is where Magnusson, Agre, and Barad land in your actual work.Try: "This tool wants me to produce ___; I will use constraint X to force it toward [a different outcome]."Address at least two of the following: What does your primary tool know — what worldview does it embed — and how is that in tension or alignment with what you're trying to make? Whose body, whose context, whose way of knowing is your apparatus built for? Is that yours? Where do you anticipate hitting the tool's wall — the limit of what it can think? How are you entangled with your tools and materials? Where is the boundary between you, the tool, and the work genuinely unclear? Loveless speaks of the "boundary object." This is a result that lives between institutional expectation and personal research identity. Both matter, and they don't always want the same thing.Be honest about the tension: What does the department/course need to see? What counts as evidence of rigor, craft, or completion in this context? What does your practice / research identity need? What would it mean for this work to be true to what's actually pulling you? These don't have to be the same thing. But naming the gap between them is useful; it helps you navigate toward something that satisfies both without collapsing into either.On uncertainty: the proposal should contain some. If you're not uncertain about anything, you're not actually speculating, you're describing a predetermined outcome. Uncertainty is evidence the inquiry is live.On revision: this document will be different at Week 10. Document your reasoning now so you can see the transformation. The gap between versions is part of the work.On format departures: if prose feels wrong for how you think, talk to me. Diagrams, annotated images, recorded audio, the format should not determine the rigor.
See also: Research-Creation thread · Enabling Constraints thread · Epistemic Tools thread
