The sphere is structurally stable in dry conditionsIDG_20260406_114518_273.jpgIDG_20260405_224124_714.jpgIMG_6597.jpegDIY Water Dissolution SubstrateAlvin Lucier | Red Bull Music AcademyUbuWeb Sound - Alvin LucierAlvin Lucier - Arts at MITAtmospheric sound. It is more “optimized” for the acoustic properties of water.Pressure waves propagating through liquidThat sound can travel through a medium that isn't air. That water has its own acoustic logic. What does it resist?What does it yield to?WORKS IN CONVERSATION What does it already know?What would it take to put this in a signal chain?DIY HydrophoneWhat does it open?What is it thinking?H5studio-2-Hero2.png.768x0_q60.png (768×768)That sound is something that can move through air: sound has amplitude (physical) sound has frequency (physical) sound has wavelength (physical)
sound can be captured as a voltage signal (physical → digital) Pasted image 20260406133443.jpgPasted image 20260406133440.jpgPasted image 20260406132830.png Each person brings one (im)material thing. We find out what it knows. This is the first collective event of the course. You brought something. I brought something. We're going to put them all in the same room and see what happens when we actually talk about them.
Collective Practice
Enabling Constraints
Physical-Digital Entanglement
Research-CreationFor each contribution we're working through the same three questions:1. What does it resist? What does it yield to? Not what it is, but what it does. What happens when you push on it? 2. What does it already know? Every material, tool, or dataset carries embedded logic: assumptions about what it's for, what it can sense, what it makes legible. What worldview is already in the thing you brought? 3. What would it take to put this in a signal chain? What sensor, protocol, or system could turn its behavior into data? What gets amplified? What gets lost?I brought three things together…What it is: A portable audio recorder with interchangeable capsule system (XY stereo capsule default) + 2 additional inputs for external mics or line sources.What it resists: It's designed to capture sound above water, through air. The diaphragm is optimized for atmospheric pressure and airborne sound waves. Submerge it and it fails. That failure is a constraint. What it yields to: Everything in its polar pattern, within its frequency response curve. It's extraordinarily accurate and faithful. Which means it also captures everything you didn't intend (room noise, handling noise, etc.). That is another of its constraints.What it knows: That sound is something that moves through air, that has amplitude and frequency, that can be captured as a voltage signal. It doesn't know about pressure differentials in water, or the acoustic signature of dissolution, or what it means for a material to "sound like" something, culturally speaking. Signal chain position: Capture device → digital audio file → DAW or Max/MSP → granular synthesis or convolution. The H5 is the first transduction point.What it is: A piezoelectric contact microphone sealed in an epoxy housing — built to go into water. Where the H5 fails, this picks up at that moment. What it resists: Atmospheric sound (it's designed to be submerged). High-frequency detail in air is lost. It is more “optimized” for the acoustic properties of water, which transmit certain frequencies differently than air. It also resists damage from submersion that would destroy a conventional diaphragm mic.What it yields to: Pressure waves propagating through liquid (including the sounds that materials make as they dissolve, swell, crack, and settle). The crackle of a substrate fracturing under water. The CO₂ fizz of an effervescent reaction. What it knows: That sound can travel through a medium that isn't air. That water has its own acoustic logic. That a piezo element converts mechanical pressure directly to voltage.Signal chain position: Hydrophone → H5 mic input → digital audio → Max/RNBO granular patch. The hydrophone acts as the second transduction: physical pressure → electrical signal. What it is: A bath bomb-style compressed “sphere” (more like loose moon-sand right now) made from baking soda, citric acid, cornstarch, clay (bentonite or kaolin), salts, and iron oxide pigment. Designed to dissolve in water over 10–40 minutes, producing acoustic, visual, and chemical events as it does. What it resists: Dissolution is its enabling constraint and its generative condition. The sphere is structurally stable in dry conditions; contact with water is the co-cause that activates its temporal properties.What it yields to: Water. Heat. Time. Each material layer artifact or suspends at a different rate. The iron oxide creates ink-like plumes The bentonite swells before dispersing, clouding the water The salt crystals fracture and dissolve with audible cracks What it knows (by design): The sphere is built from materials chosen for both their cultural and sonic resonances (obsidian black, earth tones, water-soluble minerals). For this, chemistry becomes a form of argument-in-action. The dissolution profile is activates a score. Signal chain position: Sphere in water → hydrophone captures acoustic events → H5 records → granular synthesis in Max/RNBO maps dissolution data to sound. The sphere is another instrument and the water the performance space. What does a material know; and what becomes audible when we put it in a signal chain? The H5 is designed for air. The hydrophone is designed for water. The sphere is designed to dissolve. The enabling constraint of these instruments arises from their combination. The three co-causes that produce something none of them could alone.(Populated during class — each student's object, their three-question responses, and any signal chain thinking that emerged in the room.)A few artists whose potluck logic is worth knowing:Zimoun — sound sculptures using mechanical components Simple materials (cardboard, wire, motors) combined with simple constraints (one motion, one material, repeated) to produce emergent acoustic complexity. The constraint is reductive; the result is not.
→ zimoun.netChristine Sun Kim — sound as material / Game of Skill 2.0 Kim works with sound as a material to be shaped, exploring how sound carries social power, and what it means to control vs. be controlled by sonic space as a Deaf artist. The "constraint" of Deafness becomes the condition for new forms.
→ christinesunkim.com
→ https://rhizome.org/editorial/2015/oct/30/artist-profile-christine-sun-kim/
→ https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJvys3curssMendi + Keith Obadike — Blackness for Sale (2001) / sonic practice An eBay listing offering his [Keith Obadike’s] "Blackness" for sale: the platform's auction logic is the constraint; the listing becomes a conceptual artwork about how Blackness is commodified and sold. The tool's assumptions are turned against themselves.
→ https://elmcip.net/creative-work/blackness-sale
→ https://direct.mit.edu/books/edited-volume/4374/chapter-abstract/187414/The-Black-Net-Art-Actions-Blackness-for-Sale-2001?redirectedFrom=fulltextTristan Perich — 1-Bit Symphony (2010) An entire symphony composed for a single-bit audio chip: 1 or 0, on or off, no in between. The computational constraint becomes the aesthetic. The limitation and the emergence is the timbre and msuic.
→ tristanperich.com
→ https://cantaloupemusic.com/albums/1-bit-symphony
→ https://arts.mit.edu/tristan-perichs-1-bit-symphony/
The potluck feeds directly into the workshop — W02B. You'll take what you just described and push it further: an effort to convert a limitative constraint to an enabling one, and (conceptually) put an object in the signal chain.
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — techniques of relation; the studio event as collective thinking
Magnusson — *Epistemic Tools* — amplification-reduction; tools as epistemic artifacts
DIGM 553 - W02A - (Im)material PotluckPasted image 20260407155317.png A limitation that, through interaction with other forces, generates emergence rather than just restriction. The goal today is to do our best to feel and operate an enabling constraint. We're going to work with what we brought and see what happens when we push on its limits.
Enabling Constraints
Research-Creation
Physical-Digital EntanglementFor Manning & Massumi: gravity is implacable. You can't dance without it. You can jump without it. There are many aspects of our daily lives and activates that would be impossible without it. Gravity thus, enables the possible. Now, take the jump. Add horizontal momentum and you get an arc: a collaboration between two co-causes. Neither gravity nor momentum alone makes the jump. The constraint is generative because of its resistance.The question this opens: What's the gravity in your object? What does it resist that you could push against? Place your object on the shared surface. Describe it — but you cannot use the words "material" or "art."Instead, try: What does it resist? What does it yield to? What does it amplify? What does it reduce? What can not be done with it? (That's your starting constraint.) What does it do to the thing closest to it? Pick one thing your object cannot do. One real limitation.Now: what second thing (a co-cause) could convert that limitation into generative potential?The co-cause can be: Another object or material A rule or instruction A body position or gesture A sensor or signal chain A time constraint Write down the pair: [limitation] + [co-cause] → [what becomes possible]You're designing an enabling constraint.Pick one object from the table. [Conceptually] connect your object to a sensor. (or if you have the stuff, you could actually do it)At the moment of connection: pause. Ask: What just happened to this object? What did it become? What does the sensor now "know" about the object? What doesn't it know? What's being amplified? What's being reduced? Write 2–3 sentences: what did the object become when it entered the signal chain?This is the physical-digital entanglement moment — a foreign object enters a circuit and both things change.Return to your original object. Describe it again — same no-"material"/no-"art" constraint from Round 1, but now you've been through the workshop.Did your description change? If yes: what changed it? If no: what does that tell you about how you're relating to this object?Group discussion: what's the enabling constraint of the workshop itself?A few works where the constraint is the piece, not an obstacle to it:Alvin Lucier — I Am Sitting in a Room (1969) The room's acoustic resonance is the constraint. Lucier records himself speaking, plays it back into the room, records that, plays it back again, until the room's frequencies overtake his voice entirely. The limitation (imperfect playback in a reverberant space) becomes the compositional process.
→ Listen / readNeri Oxman — Material Ecology / Silk Pavilion (2013) The constraint is the silkworm's biology: it can only spin within certain temperature and humidity ranges, following pheromone traces. Oxman designs the armature; the worms design the surface. The biological constraint shapes the architecture.
→ MIT Media Lab documentationTarek Atoui — The Reverse Collection (2016) Atoui works with Deaf and hearing-impaired communities to design instruments that bypass conventional acoustic listening. The "constraint" of non-standard hearing becomes the condition for new instrument forms.
→ Frieze profilePauline Oliveros — Deep Listening practice Not a single work, but a practice built around the constraint of duration and attention: listening so slowly and deeply that normally unnoticed sounds become material. The constraint is temporal: you are not allowed to move on.
→ Deep Listening InstituteTorkwase Dyson — Black Compositional Thought (ongoing) Dyson uses the constraint of a fixed geometric vocabulary — arcs, rectangles, horizontal planes — to think spatial liberation for Black bodies. The limitation of the vocabulary becomes the condition for specificity.
→ Artist siteAdd your own examples here as the course develops. When did a constraint in your practice stop being frustrating and start being useful? What changed? What would it mean to design your constraints before you design your content? Is there a constraint in your current project that's limitative? Could you convert it?
Describe “what your object is” in the same sense of the initial prompt — (Im)material Potluck — Prep Now, describe the object you brought to the potluck as if it were an enabling constraint. What does it resist? What co-cause would make that resistance generative? What could it become when it entered the signal chain? Or what would it become?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — Propositions 0–3
Magnusson — *Epistemic Tools* — on tools as amplification-reduction systemsDIGM 553 - W02B - Enabling Constraints WorkshopIt yields to its polar pattern + frequency response curve.What is it?

item.title: What Is Your Dog
item.description: Loveless's reading of Haraway: 'your dog' is your specific, situated, non-generalizable entry point into research. It is not a topic but a relation — the particular tangle of curiosity, material, and context that only you can follow.Research-Creation Enabling Constraints EntanglementLoveless gives us the "dog" as a figure for situated, non-generalizable knowledge. You cannot research in general. You research from somewhere specific — a body, a relation, a material entanglement you are already inside of. Haraway's original move was to say that the dog is not a metaphor for the researcher; it is the actual site of inquiry. The specificity is the method.Camus & Vinck (Part 1) extend this into practice: tools and materials are not neutral instruments that you pick up and put down. They have histories, they encode assumptions, they shape what you can notice and what you cannot. Working with a tool is working inside a worldview.The two readings together ask the same question from different angles: What have you already committed to, and do you know it?That is what the proposal is trying to surface — not a plan, but an honest account of your situated starting point.

item.title: Signal Chain Setup Guide
item.description:
Getting your microcontroller talking to your computer. From unboxing to touch data flowing into Max, TouchDesigner. This guide assumes you have hardware in hand. If you're still figuring out which sensors match your practice, start with Hardware Clarifications — Thinking Toward Sensors first.The QT Py RP2040 is the course microcontroller. It's tiny, has a built-in STEMMA QT / Qwiic connector (the 4-pin JST-SH port on the end of the board), and runs CircuitPython cleanly.Key pins to know: SDA → GPIO 22 (also labeled SDA on the board) SCL → GPIO 23 (also labeled SCL) STEMMA QT port → directly wired to SDA/SCL — no wiring needed if you use a STEMMA QT cable 3.3V and GND → available on the pin headers for anything that doesn't use STEMMA QT The RP2040 does not have built-in WiFi. This board communicates over USB serial — it sends plain text data directly to your laptop, where TouchDesigner, Max/MSP, or PlugData reads it. No intermediate script needed.The MPR121 gives you 12 capacitive touch inputs (labeled 0 through 11). Each input can be connected to any conductive material — copper tape, conductive thread, metal objects, wire — and the sensor detects when that material is touched.Key facts: I2C address: 0x5A (default). Can be changed to 0x5B, 0x5C, or 0x5D by bridging the ADDR jumper pad on the breakout — useful if you need to stack multiple MPR121s on the same bus Connects via STEMMA QT → one cable, no soldering required for basic use Electrode pads: The 0–11 pads on the breakout are where you attach conductive materials. Alligator clips, solid-core wire, or copper tape all work. CircuitPython library: adafruit_mpr121 CircuitPython is the firmware that lets you write and run Python scripts on the board. You only need to do this once.
Go to: https://circuitpython.org/board/adafruit_qtpy_rp2040/Download the latest stable .uf2 file (green "DOWNLOAD .UF2 NOW" button). Hold the BOOT button on the QT Py (the small button on the board) While holding it, plug the USB-C cable into the board and your computer Release the BOOT button The board mounts as a USB drive called RPI-RP2 Drag the .uf2 file you downloaded directly onto the RPI-RP2 drive. The board will reboot automatically.After rebooting, the board remounts as a new USB drive called CIRCUITPY. You should see a code.py file and a lib/ folder. Done.CircuitPython uses a lib/ folder on the CIRCUITPY drive. You copy library files there manually.Download the Adafruit CircuitPython Bundle from:
https://github.com/adafruit/Adafruit_CircuitPython_Bundle/releasesDownload the bundle matching your CircuitPython version (e.g., adafruit-circuitpython-bundle-10.x-mpy-YYYYMMDD.zip). Unzip it — you'll get a large folder of .mpy files.For MPR121 (required):adafruit_mpr121.mpy adafruit_connection_manager.mpy The board sends plain text over USB serial. Your receiving software (TouchDesigner, Max/MSP, or PlugData) reads that text directly — no additional libraries or scripts needed on the laptop side. Take a STEMMA QT / Qwiic cable (the small 4-pin JST cable — usually included with Adafruit breakouts, or buy separately) Plug one end into the STEMMA QT port on the QT Py RP2040 Plug the other end into either STEMMA QT port on the MPR121 breakout That's it. Power and I2C data are all on that cable. Attaching electrodes: Clip or solder a wire to any of the 0–11 pads on the MPR121 Connect the other end to your conductive material — copper tape, conductive thread, a metal object, a piece of foil pressed against something The sensor detects when conductance at that pad changes (i.e., when a human body or grounded conductor touches it) The board runs two files: boot.py (enables the USB serial data channel) and code.py (reads the MPR121 and sends touch data as plain text). Your software on the laptop reads that text directly — no bridge script needed.Save this as code.py on the CIRCUITPY drive:# DIGM 553 — Signal Chain: MPR121 capacitive touch → USB serial # Adafruit QT Py RP2040 + MPR121 12-key capacitive touch sensor # Sends touch/release events AND raw capacitance over USB for the OSC bridge import board import busio import usb_cdc import time import adafruit_mpr121 # type: ignore # ── SETUP ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── i2c = busio.I2C(board.SCL1, board.SDA1) mpr = adafruit_mpr121.MPR121(i2c) # Default I2C address 0x5A serial = usb_cdc.data # USB serial data channel # ── MAIN LOOP ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── last_touched = mpr.touched() while True: current = mpr.touched() for i in range(12): bit = 1 << i was = last_touched & bit now = current & bit # Raw capacitance: baseline minus filtered (higher = more touch pressure) baseline = mpr.baseline_data(i) filtered = mpr.filtered_data(i) raw = baseline - filtered # 0 at rest, increases with touch if not was and now: msg = f"TOUCH,{i},{raw}\n" serial.write(msg.encode()) elif was and not now: msg = f"RELEASE,{i},{raw}\n" serial.write(msg.encode()) elif now: # Continuous data while held — comment out if too noisy msg = f"RAW,{i},{raw}\n" serial.write(msg.encode()) last_touched = current time.sleep(0.01) # 100Hz polling To fix the error messages when pasting the code from here in VS Code: Open Find/Replace (Ctrl+H). Enable regex (.*). In Find, type \u00A0. Replace all with a normal space. Save. You also need to enable the USB serial data channel. Create a file called boot.py on CIRCUITPY with this content:# boot.py — enables USB serial data channel on RP2040 import usb_cdc usb_cdc.enable(console=True, data=True) After saving boot.py, unplug and replug the board for it to take effect.The board appears as two serial ports on your computer once boot.py is in place — a console port (the REPL) and a data port. You want the data port (usually the larger number).Finding the data port: Mac: run ls /dev/tty.usbmodem* in Terminal — you'll see two entries; the data port is typically the one with the higher number Windows: open Device Manager → Ports (COM & LPT) — two COM ports will appear; try the one you haven't used before Press Tab and add a Serial DAT In its parameters, set Port to your data port (e.g. /dev/cu.usbmodem... on Mac, COM4 on Windows) Set Row/Callback Format to One Per Line Set Baud Rate to 115200 (USB CDC ignores this but TD requires a value) Touch an electrode — you should see rows appearing: TOUCH,2,18, RAW,2,24, RELEASE,2,3 Press Tab and add a DAT Execute Wire your Serial DAT into it as the input In the DAT Execute parameters, turn on Row Change and turn off everything else Paste this into the script: def onRowChange(dat, rows): for row in rows: line = dat[row, 0].val.strip() if not line: continue cells = line.split(',') if len(cells) < 3: continue event = cells[0] idx = int(cells[1]) raw = int(cells[2]) table = op('/project1/electrode_state') if event == 'TOUCH': table[idx + 1, 1] = 1 table[idx + 1, 2] = raw elif event == 'RELEASE': table[idx + 1, 1] = 0 table[idx + 1, 2] = raw elif event == 'RAW': table[idx + 1, 2] = raw Now create the electrode_state Table DAT that the script writes into. Open the Textport with Alt+T and run each of these three steps separately:Step 3a — create the DAT:t = op('/project1').create(tableDAT, 'electrode_state') Step 3b — clear it and add the 12 electrode rows:t = op('/project1/electrode_state') t.clear() for i in range(12): t.appendRow([i, 0, 0]) Step 3c — insert the header row at position 0:t.insertRow(['electrode', 'state', 'raw'], 0) These must be run as three separate Textport commands — the Textport can't follow a for loop with an additional statement in the same block.You should end up with 13 rows — a header row plus one row per electrode. The insertRow(..., 0) adds the headers after the data rows so electrode 0's data never overwrites the column names.Add a DAT to CHOP after electrode_state. Each electrode becomes a named channel you can feed directly into audio, visuals, or any other part of your network:Serial DAT → DAT Execute → (writes to) electrode_state Table DAT ↓ DAT to CHOP ↓ Select CHOP → your network Use the [serial] object:[serial a 115200] ← 'a' picks the first available port; change to b, c etc. for the data port | [fromsymbol] | [zl join] | [route TOUCH RAW RELEASE] The messages arriving are plain text lines like TOUCH,2,18. Use [regexp] or [sprintf] to split on the comma and extract electrode number and raw value.In Max, open the Serial menu (Extras → Serial) to see which port letter corresponds to your data port.PlugData does not currently support serial communication reliably for this use case. The [comport] external outputs raw bytes as numbers rather than parsed text strings, meaning the TOUCH, RAW, and RELEASE message content never arrives intact — [route] has nothing to work with.Use Max/MSP or TouchDesigner instead. Both handle USB serial text correctly out of the box with no additional setup.If you are committed to a Pd-based environment, one workaround is a small Python script on your laptop that reads serial and forwards data as OSC, received in PlugData via [oscreceive]. However this reintroduces bridge script complexity and is better suited to an ESP32/Feather setup with built-in WiFi — ask your instructor if that path makes sense for your project.Board not showing up as CIRCUITPY drive → Try a different USB cable — many cables are charge-only; you need a data cable → The QT Py RP2040 uses USB-C; confirm your cable supports dataNo I2C device found / import error on MPR121 → Check the STEMMA QT cable is fully seated on both ends (they click in slightly) → Confirm adafruit_mpr121.mpy is in the lib/ folder on CIRCUITPYSerial data not arriving in Max/TD/PlugData → Make sure boot.py was saved and the board was replugged after — the data port only appears after boot.py runs → Confirm you are connected to the data port, not the console/REPL port (there will be two ports; try the other one) → On Mac the port looks like /dev/cu.usbmodem...; on Windows COM3 or similarTouch data triggering randomly / too sensitive → Tune thresholds in code.py after MPR121 init: mpr.set_thresholds(12, 6) — lower numbers = more sensitive; raise the first value to reduce false triggers → Keep electrode wires short and away from power cables where possibleOnce everything is running, here is what you have:conductive material ↓ MPR121 electrode (capacitance → threshold event) ↓ I2C → QT Py RP2040 (Python: detect change, format message) ↓ USB serial → laptop (plain text: TOUCH,2,18 / RAW,2,24 / RELEASE,2,3) ↓ Max/MSP or TouchDesigner (receive, parse, route, map) ↓ audio / visual / other output Each arrow is a transformation. Something is amplified; something is reduced. The MPR121 reduces a complex capacitance field to 12 states. The serial protocol reduces those to timestamped text strings. Max or TouchDesigner maps those strings to something audible or visible. At no point is the original touch fully preserved.

item.title: Week03-NEW
item.description:
embeds worldviewformalizes worldproduces phenomenawhose embodiment?whose critical foot?whose intra-action?what can’t it hear?stay with troubleapparatus excludesVideo LectureStudio Pulse — Magnusson Meow Wolf builds environments where the architecture is the interface. Every ramp, doorframe, and texture is an epistemic tool, it decides what counts as ‘up,’ ‘in,’ ‘weird.’Critical Technical PracticeEvery tool you use is already arguing something. It has opinions baked in, about what counts as data, what counts as sound, what a "good" output looks like. Magnusson calls these epistemic tools: instruments that don't just do things, they know things. And what they know shapes what you can think. "Instruments determine what is possible, and what is possible determines to a large extent what can be thought." TouchDesigner thinks in networks and real-time data flow. Max/MSP thinks much the same way, but more discreetly with time via messages and patches. Unity thinks in (game) objects with update loops. Each of those is a set of propositions about how the world is/should be organized. When you choose a tool, you're not picking a neutral vessel. You're entering a particular way of understanding what an interactive experience even is.Every tool amplifies something and reduces something else. The DAW amplifies the timeline, linearity, and arrangement. This idea that music has a start and end. It reduces improvisation, emergence, the idea that music is a living event. Neither is wrong. But the reduction is always there, whether you notice it or not.The question isn't "is my tool limiting me?" It always is. The question is: what is it limiting, and is that a problem for what I'm trying to make?Bluecadet builds museum and cultural experiences at scale. When they choose a platform — Unity, TouchDesigner, custom web — they're not just choosing a tool for one project. They're choosing an episteme that shapes how they interpret every brief that comes in. Their tool stack encodes what an "interactive" experience can be. Worth asking: what does Bluecadet's stack foreclose?
Meow Wolf scales experiential art into commercial spaces. Their challenge is a version of this problem too: how do you encode wonder as a repeatable, maintainable system and scale? What do their tools know about wonder that might be... wrong?
BRDG studios works smaller and more bespoke. Less infrastructure, more contingency. Their tool choices feel more situational, which means the epistemic assumptions shift project to project. Is that freedom, or is it just a different kind of constraint? Embodiment relation — you act through the tool; it recedes into the background. (You don't think about the hammer, you think about the nail.) Hermeneutic relation — the tool produces data you have to read and interpret. (The sensor gives you a number; you figure out what it means.) Alterity relation — you engage with the tool as a quasi-other, a presence you're in dialogue with. (Somax2. The model that surprises you.) Which one describes your current relationship to your primary tool? When does it shift?
Epistemic Tools Entanglement Research-CreationMagnusson, T. (2009). "Epistemic Tools: The Art of Knowing Through Making." In New Interfaces for Musical Expression.
DIGM 553 - W03A - Magnusson — Epistemic ToolsPasted image 20260414083657.pngPasted image 20260414083828.pngPasted image 20260414084026.pngPythagoras-conceived-the-universe-as-an-immense-monochord-with-its-single-string.pngWhat does your tool think? Where are you inside it? Where does it break?Computational Imperialism When a tool exports its worldview — formalizing what counts as ‘input,’ ‘event,’ ‘response’ — it starts colonizing the phenomena it was built to describe.Meow Wolf | Immersive Art Experiences & Interactive ExhibitsSplit Identity The critical programmer holds two roles at once: the making foot builds the system; the critical foot watches what the system assumes. Neither cancels the other.This is the in-class version. The formal written version becomes Journal Entry 1, due before Week 4.
See the full template and instructions here: Tool Audit — Template + GuidePick one software tool and one hardware tool from your current practice kit (or the ones you hope/plan to use in the class). Try to pick: The one you use most. The one you've stopped thinking about. Work through the audit questions. Then: find where the two tools' worldviews conflict or compound. That's where things get interesting.15 min — individual audit (both tools, quietly) 15 min — pair share: what surprised you? what did the tool assume that you never examined? 15 min — full group: collect the most surprising assumptions on the board. What patterns emerge?What does it know? What model of the world is this tool built on? What does it assume about inputs, outputs, users, bodies, time?What does it amplify? What becomes easy, fast, expressive when you use this tool?What does it reduce? What gets rounded off, hidden, made impossible?Who made the defaults? Who designed this, and for what context? Who were they imagining as the user?Where do you hit the wall? When does the tool resist what you're trying to do? What does the resistance feel like?What have you stopped questioning? What have you naturalized (made transparent or made invisible) through fluency?
Epistemic Tools Entanglement Research-CreationDIGM 553 - W03D - Epistemic Tool Audit WorkshopQ: What is one default in your current tools you have stopped questioning? What did it assume when you absorbed it?Q: Where is your split identity live right now — where are you simultaneously building and critiquing?Q: Name one moment your tool failed or glitched. What did that failure reveal about what the tool assumes?Your apparatus — as a whole — believes the world is made of certain things and not others. Today’s work: make that belief visible before it makes you.What does it know? What does it amplify? What does it discard?Failure as data Agre: stay with the bad connection. Barad: the apparatus produces what it excludes. Magnusson: what the tool can’t hear tells you what it thinks the world is.
https://vimeo.com/1183037079digm553-wk03-lecture | Videos & Movies on VimeoPasted image 20260414082903.pngNew MaterialismNew MaterialismScreenshot-e1585243380975-2281196920.pngIntra-action vs. Interaction Interaction assumes two things that pre-exist and then meet. Intra-action: the things emerge through the meeting. You and your tool are not separate before you begin.Agential Cuts Every threshold, confidence floor, and silence gap is a cut. Cuts are decision about what counts as signal and what gets discarded. Cuts enact boundaries.Entanglement + Intra-actionAgre describes what it's like to be both a builder and a critic simultaneously. He calls it a split identity: one foot in the work of making, one foot in ongoing critical reflection on what the making assumes. Not "make first, critique later." Both, at the same time, all the time.The building/technical mode wants closure. It wants to nail down the problem, define the variables, build the system. Criticism introduces instability: it keeps reopening what the technical mode wants to close. So there's a real tension. Most professional settings push hard toward the technical mode: ship it, document it, move on.Agre's argument is that the split identity isn't a luxury of academic affectation, it really cannot be. The split identity is the thing that makes practice actually good; especially in fields (like ours) where the tool choices carry such cultural, political, environmental, and epistemic weight.Every technical system contains a hidden layer: assumptions about who the user is, what bodies are like, what counts as normal behavior, what environments the system expects. These assumptions don't announce themselves. They're in the defaults. They're in what the error messages say and don't say. They're in what the system does when you do something unexpected.Agre calls this computational imperialism: the tendency of technical systems to impose their model of the world on whoever uses them, usually without acknowledgment. The user adapts to the system. The system never adapts to the user.Critical technical practice means noticing that layer. Making it visible. And sometimes working against it.The split identity is a habit. Practically, it can look like: Keeping a log of moments when you hit the wall of a tool's assumptions Naming what you had to give up to make something work inside the tool Asking "who designed these defaults, and for whom?" before naturalizing them That's what your Critical Technical Journal (CTJ) is partly asking you to do.
Epistemic Tools Entanglement Research-CreationAgre, P. (1997). "Toward a Critical Technical Practice: Lessons Learned in Trying to Reform AI." In Social Science, Technical Systems, and Cooperative Work.DIGM 553 - W03B - Agre — Critical Technical PracticeBRDG StudiosThe Apparatus Not a neutral recorder of reality but a material-discursive practice that produces the phenomena it studies. Your hydrophone + Max patch + corpus = one apparatus with one worldview.ASN 1 Component — Due: beginning of Week 5
See full assignment brief: ASN 1: Potluck + Speculative ProposalA proposal in this experimental media arts lab is not meant to be seen as a list of promised deliverables. It is more so a construction of conditions. You are aiming to act with precision (pragmatism) to catalyze the unknown (speculative). Manning and Massumi call this speculative pragmatism: the work of building a situation that allows something not yet known to happen. This document is a living artifact. It will be revised (due at Week 10). The gap between the two versions (what changed and why) is itself part of the research/processs.A PDF to Blackboard. Prose, annotated diagrams, hybrid, etc. If you wish to depart significantly from this structure, talk to me first.What is the specific, situated thing that's pulling you? A relation. A question that has you in it. Loveless, following Haraway, calls this your "dog," the particular thing you can't stop following, the pull that refuses to generalize away. Focus not on what you're making but on whom and what you are touching when you engage this process.Be specific. "I'm interested in how capacitive touch changes when the conductive surface is hair, not metal; what shifts about agency, contact, and consent" is a driving curiosity. "I'm interested in interactivity and the body" is not. Try writing: "I am obsessively inquiring into the gap between and because... What I don't understand yet is..." A map — visual or written — of the tools, materials, environments, bodies, and relations that constitute your project's technical and social apparatus. Not a list, A map. One that shows how things depend on, condition, or transform each other.Pull from your Tool Audit findings here. Locate the specific "theoretical instruments" (the audio buffers, touch thresholds, protocol choices) you're choosing to keep in your loop and why.Include: Hardware and software tools Physical materials, objects, surfaces, spaces Bodies (whose? doing what?) Data (what kind, how captured, how stored) Site or environment Protocols and signal flows Dependencies — what does X require Y for? Unknowns — things you still need to figure out A rough sketch is fine. The point is to see the whole apparatus.Define 3–5 specific, formal rules that will govern your making process. Remember: a constraint is not a limitation; it is a catalyst for surprise. They are conditions that creates productive friction without predetermining the outcome. Constraints should be typed (as in categorized). Aim for at least one of each: Technical constraint — governs your signal chain or tools (e.g., "No audio playback over 1.5 seconds.") Material constraint — governs physical or environmental conditions (e.g., "Must be triggered by physical proximity only — no keyboard/mouse input.") Affective constraint — governs relationship, attention, or intent (e.g., "Incorporate one error from the console as an intentional feature rather than a bug to fix.") For each constraint, write: The constraint: what it is, exactly Why this one: what pressure or generativity you expect from it What it forecloses: what you're giving up (a constraint that forecloses nothing isn't a constraint) Ask yourself: are your constraints based on your skills, or are they hiding your skills? Both are valid starting points, but know which one you're doing.A paragraph (or two) on the epistemics of your project. This is where Magnusson, Agre, and Barad land in your actual work.Try: "This tool wants me to produce ___; I will use constraint X to force it toward [a different outcome]."Address at least two of the following: What does your primary tool know — what worldview does it embed — and how is that in tension or alignment with what you're trying to make? Whose body, whose context, whose way of knowing is your apparatus built for? Is that yours? Where do you anticipate hitting the tool's wall — the limit of what it can think? How are you entangled with your tools and materials? Where is the boundary between you, the tool, and the work genuinely unclear? Loveless speaks of the "boundary object." This is a result that lives between institutional expectation and personal research identity. Both matter, and they don't always want the same thing.Be honest about the tension: What does the department/course need to see? What counts as evidence of rigor, craft, or completion in this context? What does your practice / research identity need? What would it mean for this work to be true to what's actually pulling you? These don't have to be the same thing. But naming the gap between them is useful; it helps you navigate toward something that satisfies both without collapsing into either.On uncertainty: the proposal should contain some. If you're not uncertain about anything, you're not actually speculating, you're describing a predetermined outcome. Uncertainty is evidence the inquiry is live.On revision: this document will be different at Week 10. Document your reasoning now so you can see the transformation. The gap between versions is part of the work.On format departures: if prose feels wrong for how you think, talk to me. Diagrams, annotated images, recorded audio, the format should not determine the rigor.
See also: Research-Creation thread · Enabling Constraints thread · Epistemic Tools threadSpeculative Proposal — Template + GuideQ: Where in your signal chain do you stop being a user and become part of the apparatus?Studio Pulse — Barad Bluecadet’s interactive installations: when visitor body + sensor + projection co-produce an event, there is an intra-action. The visitors become part of the apparatus.Q: What does your tool discard in the service of a ‘clean signal’? Is that discard compositional material?All three agree: tools embed worldviews. The question is whether you can see yours from inside it.Creative Arts & Design Studio | Poetic KineticsCreative Computing Institute | Creative Computing InstituteAtelier Lozano-HemmerBarad asks us to reconsider a pretty basic assumption: that things exist before their relations. i.e.: That you are one thing, Your tool is another thing, and Your material is yet another thing And then those things interact. They say no. The boundaries between things are not given. They are enacted through practice and relation. This is what is meant by intra-action rather than interaction.Interaction assumes two pre-formed entities coming together: you + Touchdesigner (TD), each fully formed, exchanging influence.Intra-action says: the entities emerge through the relation. The version of you that exists when you're deep in a patchwork is not the same version of you that existed before. The version of TD that exists in your practice is not the same as TD in the abstract. The practice/relation constitutes both.Barad uses the word apparatus for the whole material-discursive arrangement through which knowledge gets made. An apparatus includes the social, institutional, and conceptual structures that make a particular kind of inquiry possible (through the faculties of the object). The lab, the protocol, the grant structure, the assumptions of the field, all apparatus.For this course: your apparatus includes your hardware, your software, your studio space, your practice context, the course itself, the readings, your collaborators. That is because they are all co-constituting the phenomena you're making.
Bluecadet builds for institutions: museums, cultural centers, public spaces. Their work is entangled with architecture, with curators, with conservation concerns, with visitor behavior at scales from one person to thousands. The "tool" is never just software; it's a whole apparatus including the wall it is mounted on and the demographic of who walks past it.
Meow Wolf is an interesting case: they're a collective that became a company. Something changed in the apparatus. The entanglements shifted: new stakeholders, new financial structures, new obligations. What did that do to what was possible to make? This is Barad's point made very concrete.
BRDG studios works with clients communities where the entanglement is highly relational. The apparatus includes trust. It includes narrative and creative vision. It includes whether people in that room feel the purpose and story by what was built. That's its in the apparatus.If you are entangled with your tools, mutually constituted by them, then the tool audit is a map of the conditions of your own practice. You're not standing outside your tools observing them. You're in it. The audit is a way of trying to see something you're inside of.That's hard. It is supposed to be hard.
Epistemic Tools Entanglement Research-Creation Physical-Digital EntanglementBarad, K. (2007). Meeting the Universe Halfway: Quantum Physics and the Entanglement of Matter and Meaning. Duke University Press.DIGM 553 - W03C - Barad — Entanglement and Intra-actionNew MaterialismAmplification / Reduction Tools make some things easy and some things impossible. Invisible Architecture The most powerful design decisions are the ones you stop seeing. What have you naturalized in your signal chain without examining?Studio Pulse — Agre brdg.studio: their practice builds the computational logic in the room and asks what worldview it will present before deploying it in public space.BluecadetWhose body? Magnusson’s amplification, Agre’s marginalization, Barad’s apparatus — they all circle the same question: whose context was imagined when this was built?Black Boxes Every tool is a crystallized argument. When you stop questioning the default, the designer's choice becomes invisible, and starts shaping yours.Ihde’s Modalities Embodiment — tool disappears into use Hermeneutic — tool mediates interpretation Alterity — tool becomes an ‘other’ you relate to
Epistemic ToolsPasted image 20260414084208.pngbLxtp8rUsHNb4kBlLoOAxz9vO0-3213374487.pngJournal Entry 1 — Epistemic Tool Audit
Part of ASN 2: Critical Technical Journal, Installment 1The Epistemic Tool Audit (ETA) is a structured anatomy of your project's apparatus. You are going to be asking what your tools think, where you are inside the apparatus, and where the tools break (or impasse).Building on Agre and Magnusson, this exercise rejects the idea of tools as neutral intermediaries. The hardware, software, and protocol that make up your signal chain encode worldviews, prescribe behaviors, and quietly marginalize alternative ways of knowing. This audit is one way in which we can that invisible visible.Core inquiry: What does my tool think? Where am I inside it? Where does it break?Before you audit anything, map your primary signal chain: [Input Hardware] → [Protocol] → [Output Software] Document it physically (a photo) and virtually (a screenshot). This is the apparatus you're auditing, the entire whole loop.Map your loop against four research lenses. For each cell, write one analytic sentence. Don't aim for completeness — aim for honesty. Blanks are data too.After completing the matrix, write one paragraph answering: what does this apparatus — as a whole — believe the world is? What behavior is it incentivizing? Who does it want you to be: a conductor, a coder, a consumer? What part of your artistic intent doesn't fit its parameters — what gets tossed to make a clean signal? If the matrix opens something you want to follow further, these questions can extend the work:On worldview (Magnusson): What behavior is the tool incentivizing? Does it want me to be a conductor, a coder, or a consumer?On marginalization (Agre): What part of my intent doesn't "fit" into the parameters of this tool? What gets discarded in the service of a clean, functional signal?On entanglement (Barad/Loveless): Where do my habits blend into the gain-knob or the slider? Since I cannot measure something without changing it; how is my touch changing the signal?On translation (Magnusson): What is happening when "sound" becomes "math," when gesture becomes data, when touch becomes a threshold value? What dies in the handshake? IN other words, what gets lost/reduced?Once you've worked through the matrix, write a short synthesis (it could be a paragraph or a mapped diagram) on where the tools' worldviews converge, conflict, or compound: Where do they align? Do they share a cosmology? Where do they conflict? Do they pull in different directions? Where do they compound? Do they reinforce each other's reductions in ways that are easy to miss? What does the friction open up? "The moment I realized this tool had a worldview was when..." "The default that surprised me most was..." "This tool was designed for someone who..." "When I try to do ___, I have to fight the tool because..." "These two tools agree that the world is... but I'm not sure I agree." "What escapes the signal chain entirely is..." Part of ASN 2, Installment 1. Due: beginning of Week 4. Format is flexible: written, annotated diagram, voice memo, video log. Whatever lets you think. However, the submitted document needs to be a PDF to Blackboard.Use this to map both tools side by side at a glance. Fill in what you can.
See also: Epistemic Tools thread · Entanglement threadTool Audit — Template + Guide

item.title: ETA-SpeculativeProposal
item.description: Boundry ObjectPositioningFSIWMMSWThe TerminusThe sphere is completely dissolved. The vessel contains only water, sediment, and suspended pigment. The Somax2 players have received their last phrase and are waiting for the next input, that may never come. The system holds at a final sustained note, until I stop the transport.That moment of held-note-waiting is the cryosleep. The instrument doesn't know the journey is over.The dissolution sphere's swelling phase — the expansion before dissolution — produces micro-pressure events the hydrophone can register. That swelling is a fugitive state: the sphere becoming something else before it becomes nothing.The buffer threshold default was calibrated for human generated music music. Dissolution events may produce dense and complex fizz bursts with no silence for minutes, meaning S2 never receives a phrase or a pause. The handshake breakdown IS the work of cryosleep: suspended, undelivered, constant, and ephemeral.The P1 → P2 feedback loop in s2-players is currently OFF by default. This is the most speculative gesture in the patch: each player begins to hear itself through the others, dissolving individual voice into a chorus. Enabling it is a compositional risk worth taking.DataKnot's descriptor model was built for percussive and pitched musical events (speech, instruments, onsets). It knows how to hear a drum hit. Dissolution is diffuse, broadband, chaotic, often below noise floor. The protocol's memory is of a different sonic world and understanding, one that is for more “standard” and musical.Somax2 was designed for musical improvisation — human musicians, trained musical corpus, call-and-response at human tempo. Its pattern-matching logic carries the memory of that context. The NASA corpus and spirituals corpus were not what it was built for. That friction is live and difficult to navigate; require some creative modifications.The bath bomb substrate carries industrial and manufactured assumptions about dissolution and the use of earthen material for selfcare. Relaxation, luxury, self-care. The sphere's chemistry (citric acid + baking soda) is commercially standard. What it does NOT know: that the water it enters is not meant for relaxation; it is the Atlantic, carrying centuries of trauma.Is the gap between what dk.onset~ registers and what the sphere carries compositional content — or a limitation to work around?Sensory WorldingThe hydrophone is cold and fragile held in water. The piezo disc pressed into epoxy is an instrument meat to monitor the d body in solution. It understands the water's materiality before it hears it.The OSC bus is invisible. The DataKnot onset trigger fires silently via it representation of reality. There a moment the descriptor value crosses a threshold.Max's GUI enforces a particular aesthetic of legibility — patch cables, number boxes, toggle states. It wants you to see the logic. But the dissolution event is happening in the vessel; what the GUI shows is a translation two steps removed.The DIY hydrophone epoxy seal is somewhat uncertain, it could fail in extended immersion. Recipe A produces loud bubbling hydrophone events they may saturate the ADC input. Both “failures” are materials of the work to be navigated.The pitch confidence gate (> 0.45) silently discards dissolution sounds it deems 'too noisy' or out of time. What it's discarding is certain sounds of the structural breakdown. Staying with the trouble here means lowering the confidence floor, and letting more uncontrollable noise in.What does this apparatus think the world is?HARDWARE SITEHydrophone (DIY piezo) Dissolution sphere (bath bomb substrate) Glass/acrylic vessel array (cryopod) ESP32 / Grove sensors (TDS, turbidity, temp) Zoom H5 (documentation + capture)PROTOCOL SITEFluCoMa (via DataKnot) analysis (dk.onset~, dk.pitch~, dk.loudness~, dk.spectralshape~) OSC / UDP (send/receive busses within Max) MIDI (dk-midi-bridge → phrase-buffer → Somax2) Global transport (60 BPM, 4/4, breathing 54–66)SOFTWARE SITEMax/MSP (master patch + subpatches) Data Knot / FluCoMa (dk-drone + dk-midi-bridge) Somax2 (3-player inter-agent corpus navigation) VST instruments (strings / woodwinds / piano-vib) NASA corpus + water spirituals corpusFugitive SpeculationMaterial MemoryIntimate WitnessingWhen Somax2 exceeds 80% CPU during dense dissolution phases, it produces audible silences/pauses during latency spikes. Read this as system's pattern-recognition logic being genuinely overwhelmed by the material event. Work with that overflow as one truth of the piece."I am obsessively inquiring into the gap between the material dissolution of an object in water and Somax2's representation of that dissolution, because the system can hear a fizz event and respond to it, but it cannot hear the the events of the Middle Passage long past. It cannot hear cryosleep as a fantastical representation of Black bodies in states of suspension. What I don't understand yet is: can the gap between what the tool registers and what the material carries become the compositional site itself?"This apparatus believes the world is made of detectable events — discrete onsets, pitch values above a confidence floor, phrases bounded by silence. It was built to catch things that arrive cleanly and respond with pattern in kind. What the Middle Passage produced; bodies that didn't arrive, voices that dissolved before they could be heard, signals lost in the water. All of these fall structurally below the threshold. The work attempts to performs it.THE APPARATUS \ LOOPOrganic Memory Triptych — Movement IIThe apparatus is the instrument. What does the signal chain think the world is? And what does it foreclose about how a Black body moves through water, time, and space?The pitch confidence gate is currently set at 0.45. it is discarding some of the structurally interesting dissolution sounds. What is lost in that handshake?What happens to Somax2's pattern-matching when the corpus is NASA + spirituals + dissolution? Does it make coherent phrases or noise?Technical Constraint No audio playback sourced from outside what the “built” vessel (the material and its sensors) perceives (no additional instruments). All sound-making events must originate from the dissolution event itself. Somax2's responses are the only sonic addition, and they must emerge from the corpus of selected.Why: Forces the chemical rate of the sphere to set the compositional tempo. Prohibits me from 'filling in' compositional gaps with too much pre-composed musical material. Forecloses: Pre-recorded ambience, drone bed as safety net.Material Constraint Each performance uses a new, unrepeatable sphere. No sphere is used twice. Molds can be reused but each cast is unique in its material composition specifics.Why: The sphere is a body. Bodies are not reusable instruments. Each dissolution is singular and irrecoverable. This is the temporal logic of the Middle Passage, not the loop logic of sample-based music. Forecloses: Repeatability, A/B testing of the same sphere, 'standardized' conditions.Affective Constraint During performance, I do not adjust the signal chain once the sphere enters the water. Whatever the apparatus registers, it registers. Whatever it fails to register, it fails to register.Why: Agre's split identity, specifically: the critical foot cannot intervene during the material event. The critique is written here, in this document (and will be in the subsequent reflections). In performance, the making foot holds still. Forecloses: Live patching, threshold adjustment, any real-time rescue of 'bad' data.What the committee needs to see: Evidence that the apparatus is functional and intentional. A signal chain that works. Sensor-to-synthesis mappings that are documented and defensible. A compositional logic that can be articulated in prose via a research design framework.What the practice needs: A dissolution event that doesn't resolve. A Somax2 response that can't catch what's happening in the water, but still make musical sense enough of it to respond. A performance that demonstrates the epistemological limit of pattern-recognition as a model for dissolved and disparate memories.The tension: The committee wants a working system. The work requires a system that fails in specific and meaningful ways. The proposal is to build both: the functional apparatus AND the documented failure as compositional and theoretical content.Max/MSP wants me to be a coder , a builder of logic, a designer of routing systems. Somax2 wants me to be a performer, someone who provides “influence” and receives “response” in feedback. DataKnot wants me to be an analyst, someone who extracts features from audio signals.None of these roles accounts for what I am: a Black practitioner asking a Black speculative question about a technology of suspension that the apparatus cannot alone theorize. My body is not legible to the pitch confidence gate. The Middle Passage is not in the Somax2 corpus.The epistemic position I'm working from is not against the tools, it is attempting to negotiate the friction between what they know and what I'm bringing them. The gap between what dk.onset~ detects and what the dissolution sphere carries is part of the dissertation site.

item.title: Barad — Entanglement and Intra-action
item.description:
Barad asks us to reconsider a pretty basic assumption: that things exist before their relations. i.e.: That you are one thing, Your tool is another thing, and Your material is yet another thing And then those things interact. They say no. The boundaries between things are not given. They are enacted through practice and relation. This is what is meant by intra-action rather than interaction.Interaction assumes two pre-formed entities coming together: you + Touchdesigner (TD), each fully formed, exchanging influence.Intra-action says: the entities emerge through the relation. The version of you that exists when you're deep in a patchwork is not the same version of you that existed before. The version of TD that exists in your practice is not the same as TD in the abstract. The practice/relation constitutes both.Barad uses the word apparatus for the whole material-discursive arrangement through which knowledge gets made. An apparatus includes the social, institutional, and conceptual structures that make a particular kind of inquiry possible (through the faculties of the object). The lab, the protocol, the grant structure, the assumptions of the field, all apparatus.For this course: your apparatus includes your hardware, your software, your studio space, your practice context, the course itself, the readings, your collaborators. That is because they are all co-constituting the phenomena you're making.Bluecadet builds for institutions: museums, cultural centers, public spaces. Their work is entangled with architecture, with curators, with conservation concerns, with visitor behavior at scales from one person to thousands. The "tool" is never just software; it's a whole apparatus including the wall it is mounted on and the demographic of who walks past it.
Meow Wolf is an interesting case: they're a collective that became a company. Something changed in the apparatus. The entanglements shifted: new stakeholders, new financial structures, new obligations. What did that do to what was possible to make? This is Barad's point made very concrete.
BRDG studios works with clients communities where the entanglement is highly relational. The apparatus includes trust. It includes narrative and creative vision. It includes whether people in that room feel the purpose and story by what was built. That's its in the apparatus.If you are entangled with your tools, mutually constituted by them, then the tool audit is a map of the conditions of your own practice. You're not standing outside your tools observing them. You're in it. The audit is a way of trying to see something you're inside of.That's hard. It is supposed to be hard.
Epistemic Tools Entanglement Research-Creation Physical-Digital EntanglementBarad, K. (2007). Meeting the Universe Halfway: Quantum Physics and the Entanglement of Matter and Meaning. Duke University Press.

item.title: Tool Audit — Template + Guide
item.description:
Journal Entry 1 — Epistemic Tool Audit Part of ASN 2: Critical Technical Journal, Installment 1The Epistemic Tool Audit (ETA) is a structured anatomy of your project's apparatus. You are going to be asking what your tools think, where you are inside the apparatus, and where the tools break (or impasse).Building on Agre and Magnusson, this exercise rejects the idea of tools as neutral intermediaries. The hardware, software, and protocol that make up your signal chain encode worldviews, prescribe behaviors, and quietly marginalize alternative ways of knowing. This audit is one way in which we can that invisible visible.Core inquiry: What does my tool think? Where am I inside it? Where does it break?Before you audit anything, map your primary signal chain: [Input Hardware] → [Protocol] → [Output Software] Document it physically (a photo) and virtually (a screenshot). This is the apparatus you're auditing, the entire whole loop.Map your loop against four research lenses. For each cell, write one analytic sentence. Don't aim for completeness — aim for honesty. Blanks are data too.After completing the matrix, write one paragraph answering: what does this apparatus — as a whole — believe the world is? What behavior is it incentivizing? Who does it want you to be: a conductor, a coder, a consumer? What part of your artistic intent doesn't fit its parameters — what gets tossed to make a clean signal? If the matrix opens something you want to follow further, these questions can extend the work:On worldview (Magnusson): What behavior is the tool incentivizing? Does it want me to be a conductor, a coder, or a consumer?On marginalization (Agre): What part of my intent doesn't "fit" into the parameters of this tool? What gets discarded in the service of a clean, functional signal?On entanglement (Barad/Loveless): Where do my habits blend into the gain-knob or the slider? Since I cannot measure something without changing it; how is my touch changing the signal?On translation (Magnusson): What is happening when "sound" becomes "math," when gesture becomes data, when touch becomes a threshold value? What dies in the handshake? IN other words, what gets lost/reduced?Once you've worked through the matrix, write a short synthesis (it could be a paragraph or a mapped diagram) on where the tools' worldviews converge, conflict, or compound: Where do they align? Do they share a cosmology? Where do they conflict? Do they pull in different directions? Where do they compound? Do they reinforce each other's reductions in ways that are easy to miss? What does the friction open up? "The moment I realized this tool had a worldview was when..." "The default that surprised me most was..." "This tool was designed for someone who..." "When I try to do ___, I have to fight the tool because..." "These two tools agree that the world is... but I'm not sure I agree." "What escapes the signal chain entirely is..." Part of ASN 2, Installment 1. Due: beginning of Week 4. Format is flexible: written, annotated diagram, voice memo, video log. Whatever lets you think. However, the submitted document needs to be a PDF to Blackboard.Use this to map both tools side by side at a glance. Fill in what you can.
See also: Epistemic Tools thread · Entanglement thread

item.description:
About the Course DIGM 553 is a graduate-level studio course in which students experiment with emerging tools and techniques, applying their creative vision through a research-creation methodology. This course encourages risk-taking and exploration — the process of making is the inquiry. Key themes: Research-Creation — critical inquiry and creative production as co-constitutive Epistemic Tools — tools are not neutral; they encode worldviews Entanglement — practitioner, tool, and material are mutually constituted Enabling Constraints — productive limitation as generative force Physical-Digital Entanglement — sensors, microcontrollers, and software environments Instructor: Darren Woodland, Jr. Email: dkw34@drexel.edu
Office Hours: By appointment — Microsoft Bookings

item.title: Agre — Critical Technical Practice
item.description: Agre describes what it's like to be both a builder and a critic simultaneously. He calls it a split identity: one foot in the work of making, one foot in ongoing critical reflection on what the making assumes. Not "make first, critique later." Both, at the same time, all the time.The building/technical mode wants closure. It wants to nail down the problem, define the variables, build the system. Criticism introduces instability: it keeps reopening what the technical mode wants to close. So there's a real tension. Most professional settings push hard toward the technical mode: ship it, document it, move on.Agre's argument is that the split identity isn't a luxury of academic affectation, it really cannot be. The split identity is the thing that makes practice actually good; especially in fields (like ours) where the tool choices carry such cultural, political, environmental, and epistemic weight.Every technical system contains a hidden layer: assumptions about who the user is, what bodies are like, what counts as normal behavior, what environments the system expects. These assumptions don't announce themselves. They're in the defaults. They're in what the error messages say and don't say. They're in what the system does when you do something unexpected.Agre calls this computational imperialism: the tendency of technical systems to impose their model of the world on whoever uses them, usually without acknowledgment. The user adapts to the system. The system never adapts to the user.Critical technical practice means noticing that layer. Making it visible. And sometimes working against it.The split identity is a habit. Practically, it can look like: Keeping a log of moments when you hit the wall of a tool's assumptions Naming what you had to give up to make something work inside the tool Asking "who designed these defaults, and for whom?" before naturalizing them That's what your Critical Technical Journal (CTJ) is partly asking you to do.Epistemic Tools Entanglement Research-CreationAgre, P. (1997). "Toward a Critical Technical Practice: Lessons Learned in Trying to Reform AI." In Social Science, Technical Systems, and Cooperative Work.

item.title: Magnusson — Epistemic Tools
item.description:
Every tool you use is already arguing something. It has opinions baked in, about what counts as data, what counts as sound, what a "good" output looks like. Magnusson calls these epistemic tools: instruments that don't just do things, they know things. And what they know shapes what you can think. "Instruments determine what is possible, and what is possible determines to a large extent what can be thought." TouchDesigner thinks in networks and real-time data flow. Max/MSP thinks much the same way, but more discreetly with time via messages and patches. Unity thinks in (game) objects with update loops. Each of those is a set of propositions about how the world is/should be organized. When you choose a tool, you're not picking a neutral vessel. You're entering a particular way of understanding what an interactive experience even is.Every tool amplifies something and reduces something else. The DAW amplifies the timeline, linearity, and arrangement. This idea that music has a start and end. It reduces improvisation, emergence, the idea that music is a living event. Neither is wrong. But the reduction is always there, whether you notice it or not.The question isn't "is my tool limiting me?" It always is. The question is: what is it limiting, and is that a problem for what I'm trying to make?Bluecadet builds museum and cultural experiences at scale. When they choose a platform — Unity, TouchDesigner, custom web — they're not just choosing a tool for one project. They're choosing an episteme that shapes how they interpret every brief that comes in. Their tool stack encodes what an "interactive" experience can be. Worth asking: what does Bluecadet's stack foreclose?
Meow Wolf scales experiential art into commercial spaces. Their challenge is a version of this problem too: how do you encode wonder as a repeatable, maintainable system and scale? What do their tools know about wonder that might be... wrong?
BRDG studios works smaller and more bespoke. Less infrastructure, more contingency. Their tool choices feel more situational, which means the epistemic assumptions shift project to project. Is that freedom, or is it just a different kind of constraint? Embodiment relation — you act through the tool; it recedes into the background. (You don't think about the hammer, you think about the nail.) Hermeneutic relation — the tool produces data you have to read and interpret. (The sensor gives you a number; you figure out what it means.) Alterity relation — you engage with the tool as a quasi-other, a presence you're in dialogue with. (Somax2. The model that surprises you.) Which one describes your current relationship to your primary tool? When does it shift?
Epistemic Tools Entanglement Research-CreationMagnusson, T. (2009). "Epistemic Tools: The Art of Knowing Through Making." In New Interfaces for Musical Expression.
