See Readings for full citations.Week 11Spring 2026A map of the course's entanglements — weeks and their conceptual threads.BEGINENDMaking and thinking as the same act — not phases, not sequence, not illustration.The standard model: you research something, then you make something that shows what you found. Research-creation refuses that split. Manning & Massumi locate it at what they call the prebifurcation point — the moment before making and thinking get separated into different institutional categories with different evaluation criteria. At that point, making is thinking, and thinking is already a practice.The thing this rules out is the communication model — the idea that your creative work is "delivering" research results you already had. If the project knows its outcome before it starts, it's not research-creation. The work has to be genuinely open to something it couldn't have predicted.What that actually requires in practice: conditioning rather than framing. Framing means you set up a structure and the work fills it in. Conditioning means you bring things into contact — materials, tools, questions, bodies, sensors — and stay open to what emerges from their interaction. Neither you nor any individual element fully determines the outcome.For this course: the journal is not documentation of a separate making process. The making is not an illustration of the thinking. They interpenetrate, or it's not research-creation.
Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9, Week 10, Week 11 Where in your workflow do making and thinking actually happen at the same time? Can you work from that moment deliberately? Is your project conditioned or framed? What are you holding open, and what are you predetermining? If your practice is already "thinking something" — what is it thinking right now? What in your institution (program, discipline, grading rubric) separates your thinking from your making? How do you work inside that without just reproducing it?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — Propositions 0–3.
Loveless — *Haraway's Dog* — on curiosity as a research method; following a question rather than testing a hypothesis.
Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   Entanglement   Failure as Method   Making PublicResearch-CreationTools are not neutral. Every instrument encodes a worldview — a set of propositions about what the world is, what can be known about it, and who that knowledge is for.Magnusson, drawing on Hankins & Silverman and Don Ihde, argues that instruments don't merely follow theory — they often determine it, because "instruments determine what is possible, and what is possible determines to a large extent what can be thought." An epistemic tool is any instrument understood this way: as a knowledge-making artifact with its own claims built in.Ihde identifies three modalities of how instruments mediate between body and world: embodiment relations (you act through the tool, which recedes), hermeneutic relations (the tool produces data you must interpret), and alterity relations (you engage with the tool as a quasi-other). These aren't fixed categories — any practice oscillates between them, and the shift matters.Every tool also performs an amplification-reduction: it amplifies certain features of the world and systematically reduces others. The danger isn't reduction itself — all tools must reduce. The danger is when the reduction becomes invisible, when it gets naturalized into what Latour calls a black box: an object whose internal contingency has disappeared through repeated use. Fluency closes black boxes. The critique foot of Agre's split identity keeps reopening them.
Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5 What does your primary tool amplify — what becomes easy, visible, measurable? And what does it reduce — what disappears, gets rounded off, or can't be represented? Who designed the defaults in your software? What assumptions about bodies, practices, and contexts are baked into those choices? Which of Ihde's three modalities describes your relationship to your tool right now? When does it shift — and what triggers the shift? What's the most naturalized tool in your practice — the one you've stopped questioning? What would happen if you opened that black box?
Magnusson — *Epistemic Tools* — the source text for the concept; covers Ihde's modalities, amplification-reduction, and the techne/episteme distinction.
Agre — *Critical Technical Practice* — on computational imperialism, the split identity, and the practice of making the invisible assumptions of tools visible.
Research-Creation   Enabling Constraints   Entanglement   Physical-Digital Entanglement   Failure as MethodEpistemic ToolsA constraint that opens things up rather than just closing them down.Manning & Massumi's example: gravity. You can't dance without gravity — remove it and there's no jump, no landing, no arc. Gravity is implacable, but it's also what makes the jump possible. Add horizontal momentum and "the arc of the jump will be a collaboration between the action of gravity and the energy and angular momentum of the horizontal movement acting as co-causes." That's an enabling constraint in action — resistance that generates something rather than just blocking it.The key distinction is between limitative constraints (dead ends) and enabling ones (co-causes). A limitative constraint just says stop. An enabling constraint pushes back in a way that makes something happen that wouldn't otherwise. The trick is figuring out which you're dealing with — and sometimes, how to convert one into the other.This shows up everywhere in the course. The MPR121 has 12 channels — that's a constraint, but it's also the specific sculptural logic of the thing. OSC over UDP drops packets — that's a constraint, but it forces real-time compositional decisions you wouldn't otherwise have to make. The 3-hour session is a constraint; it's also what allows the kind of depth you can't get in 50 minutes.
Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 8 What's the gravity in your practice — the resistance you can't remove? Is it enabling or just limitative? What would it take to convert it? What's the difference between a constraint someone handed you and one you designed yourself? When you hit a wall, is it a dead end or a co-cause waiting to be found? What if you designed your constraints before you designed the content?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — Propositions 0–3.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Entanglement   Failure as Method   Physical-Digital EntanglementEnabling ConstraintsPractitioner, tool, and material do not interact as pre-formed, separate entities. They are mutually constituted through the practice itself. You don't bring a self to a tool — the self that acts is partly made by the act.Barad's posthumanist performativity replaces interaction (between pre-existing things) with intra-action (the process through which distinct agencies emerge). An apparatus — for Barad, any material-discursive arrangement that makes knowledge possible — doesn't just measure or represent phenomena; it participates in producing them. The researcher, the instrument, and the phenomenon are all co-constituted through the apparatus.For this course, that means: you are not a stable subject using a neutral tool to study an external object. You are entangled with your hardware, your software, your materials, and the site of your practice. These entanglements are not metaphors — they are structural features of how knowledge gets made. Documenting them honestly is part of what the Critical Technical Journal is for.Camus & Vinck extend this into digital materiality: the digital is not immaterial. It is made of matter — servers, cables, electricity, screen light. Every "digital" thing has a thickness, a weight, a set of dependencies. The click is a material event. The file is an inscription on physical media. Recognizing this thickness is how you stop treating your tools as transparent windows onto some other reality.
Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9 What are you entangled with in your current project — not just using, but mutually constituted by? What would change about the project if that entanglement changed? Barad replaces "interaction" with "intra-action." What's the difference? Try to locate an intra-action — a moment where the boundaries between you, your tool, and your material were genuinely unclear. Where does the "digital" in your practice have material weight — consume power, require infrastructure, produce heat, leave traces? If your apparatus (the whole material-discursive arrangement of your practice) is not just measuring phenomena but helping produce them — what phenomena is yours producing?
Camus + Vinck — *Unfolding Digital Materiality* — on the thickness of digital objects; the materiality of inscription and infrastructure.
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — the concept of co-causality and conditioning is entanglement in practice.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   Physical-Digital Entanglement   Failure as MethodEntanglementFailure and impasse are not obstacles to the project. They are data about the project — revealing the formative conditions, hidden assumptions, and structural tensions that define what the work is actually doing.Agre's concept of the hassle is foundational here: not a one-time crash, but a recurring friction — something that keeps happening at the same point in your workflow, for reasons you can't quite name. Hassles are worth writing down. They are the system telling you something structural about the gap between how your tool models the world and how the world actually works.The move Agre names — and this course practices — is to treat impasse as an intellectual resource. When something fails repeatedly, don't just fix it and move on. Ask: what assumption was I making that this failure is disconfirming? What was I treating as settled that isn't? These are the questions the Critical Technical Journal is built to hold.Manning & Massumi's concept of immanent critique is also relevant here: failure, encountered from inside the practice, reveals the pressure points of the system. You can't see those pressure points from outside. You find them by building, hitting walls, and noticing where the resistance is structural rather than incidental.
Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9 What's a recurring friction in your current workflow — not a one-off problem, but something that keeps coming back? What is that hassle about? What assumption does it keep bumping against? When you hit a dead end in a project, how do you usually respond? Do you route around it, sit with it, or abandon it? What would it look like to study it instead? What's the difference between a failure that tells you something and one that doesn't? How do you tell them apart in the moment? If you had to name your most productive creative failure — the one that most changed how you work — what would you call it? What intermediation term would Agre give it?
Agre — *Critical Technical Practice* — the source of the hassle concept and the method of treating recurring friction as intellectual data.
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — immanent critique as the practice of finding pressure points from inside the system.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   Entanglement   Collective PracticeFailure as MethodPhysical and digital aren't two separate domains with an interface between them. They're entangled — each one shaping the other.The signal chain at the center of this course — body → sensor → microcontroller → protocol → software → output — is not a pipeline that converts physical reality into digital representation. It's a series of transformations. At each arrow, something is amplified and something is reduced. The body that touches a capacitive sensor is not the same as the threshold-crossing event the sensor registers. The OSC message is not the gesture. Something is always gained; something is always lost. The question is whether you know which — and whether that choice is deliberate.Magnusson puts it directly: the digital system is "material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." All three layers are active at once. The hardware has physical affordances that shape where you can put it and what it can touch. The firmware has timing properties that shape resolution and latency. The software has representational assumptions that shape what the data means. None of these layers is neutral; together they constitute the instrument.This thread tracks how physical and digital forces meet, condition each other, and produce something neither could alone — across hardware choices, material selections, installation environments, and bodies moving through space.
Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9, Week 10 At each arrow in your signal chain, what's being amplified and what's being reduced? Is that tradeoff intentional? What does your system not know about the body it's sensing — and what can happen in that gap? Where does the physical environment shape the digital behavior, and vice versa? Can you design the entanglement rather than just inheriting it? What material are your sensors touching? What cultural or social charge does that material carry — and does your system acknowledge it?
Magnusson — *Epistemic Tools* — on instruments as material-electric-symbolic systems.
Camus + Vinck — *Unfolding Digital Materiality* — on the thickness and materiality of digital objects.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   EntanglementPhysical-Digital EntanglementRendering work public is not the delivery of results. It is a continuation of the research — a way of making the formative conditions and processual transformation of the work available for encounter.Loveless, working through Haraway, argues that research-creation carries an obligation to render research public — not as a finished product submitted to evaluation, but as a practice in itself. What gets made public is not just the artifact but the forces that formed it: the impasses, the enabling constraints, the entanglements, the tools and their reductions. This is why the Final Presentation in this course is not a showcase. It is a rendering.The distinction Loveless makes is between transparency (showing your work) and accountability (taking responsibility for what your work does in the world — including what it can't do, what it excludes, and who it speaks to or past). Accountability requires knowing the stakes of the work, not just the process.For experimental media practice, making public also means confronting the question of audience: who is this for? What does it ask of the people who encounter it? A TouchDesigner patch sent to a hard drive is not public; the same patch running in a gallery space with bodies moving through it is. The difference is not technical. It is relational — and designing that relation is itself a creative and ethical act.
Week 6, Week 9, Week 11 What would it mean to make your process public — not just your result? What would you have to show that you've been hiding? Who is the audience for your work, and what does it ask of them? Have you designed that ask, or inherited it from the format? Loveless distinguishes transparency from accountability. Where in your practice are you being transparent (showing your method) without being accountable (owning what the work does or fails to do)? What form is your work made public in, and what does that form assume about who can access it?
Loveless — *Haraway's Dog* — on the obligation to render research public, curiosity as method, and the boundary object.
Research-Creation   Collective Practice   Failure as Method   EntanglementMaking PublicThe studio is not a bunch of individual practices running in parallel. It's a site where practitioners condition each other.Manning & Massumi describe the seminar or studio as an experiment: "For an 'event' to be an event, it is necessary that a collective thinking process be enacted that can give rise to new thoughts through the interaction on site." The key condition: what happens can't be predetermined. If the instructor already knows what conclusions are going to be reached and is just delivering them — that's not an event in this sense.The critique is the most direct version of this. In this course, critique is not judgment. It's activation — attending to someone else's work closely enough to surface what it's doing that it might not know it's doing. A good critique question doesn't say "this works / this doesn't." It opens something: what is this committed to? What does it refuse? What would happen if you followed that refusal further?There's an ethic here too. What you bring to the room — your presence, attention, honest response — is a contribution to a shared environment, not optional. This is part of how the work actually gets made.
Week 2, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9, Week 11 What's the difference between a critique that evaluates and one that activates? What does an activating question actually sound like? What do you bring to the room that no one else does? What does the group gain from your specific presence? When you encounter someone else's work, what's your first instinct — assess it, identify with it, question it? What would it mean to just attend to it first? How does your practice change when it's in dialogue? What has a peer's question ever revealed to you about your own work?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — on the studio event and techniques of relation.

item.title: Research-Creation Cascade — Inspirational Examples
item.description:
Kinect(v2) + Dancer + Designer ↓ Live gesture data → generative pattern + particles → procedural soundscape ↓ Unreal Engine + TouchDesigner → sound + image responseNow: what would your cascade look like?Start with your practice thinking. Work toward data. Let the sensor follow.→ Thinking Toward SensorsHomeEchoes of Harmonic ThreadsBlack bodies and narratives driven by continually perpetuated historical traumas as expressed the the entanglements of sound, dance, and Afrofuturistic narrative.Movement + Afrofuturism → purpose built hydrophones as musical ←→ cultural ←→ scientific instrumentsThe Kinect (v2) abstracts movement into gesturally recognized skeletal figures that provide points of data along the landmarks of the body.Pulse Room (2006)Every visitor who has been here is still present — their heartbeat still in the room. What would it mean to make presence accumulate rather than vanish?The body at rest → pulse / heart rate → continuous biometric streamThe most intimate involuntary signal: a heartbeat. Data the body produces without thinking. Completely individual, completely universal.Very Nervous System (1982–1991)What if the body could play an instrument not by touching it, but by moving through space? What is the instrument, if the instrument is the air itself?Presence + movement → optical flow from videoThe camera reads motion vectors — not what the body looks like, but how it is moving. Velocity and direction become the raw material.Pulse oximeter sensors (visitors hold a handle) ↓ Custom real-time system ↓ 300 incandescent bulbs — each pulsing at the rhythm of a past visitor. Newest arrival displaces the oldest heartbeat.Rafael Lozano-Hemmer - Pulse RoomVideo camera + frame grabber (built 1982 — before Max/MSP existed) ↓ Custom C software → synthesizer control signals ↓ Movement generates sound in real time — no touch, no controller, no stage equipmentVery Nervous System (1982-1991) by David Rokeby | Videos & Movies on Vimeo
https://vimeo.com/8120954?fl=pl&fe=cm
https://www.lozano-hemmer.com/pulse_room.phpCustom gloves (flex sensors, IMUs, WiFi module) ↓ Max/MSP + custom gesture mapping software ↓ Real-time synthesis, effects, looping, and arrangement — the hands become the studioMiMU | Home
https://mimugloves.comMi.Mu GlovesPerformance should be fully embodied. Why do singers stand static at a mic while all the sonic shaping happens offstage, invisible? The gesture should be the instrument.Hand + finger position, orientation, gesture → flex sensor readings + accelerometer/gyroscope dataA vocabulary of gesture mapped to a vocabulary of sound. Moving a wrist is composing.HARDWARE → SOFTWARE What transduces and processes?THE WORK What becomes possible?PRACTICE THINKING What is the work obsessed with?PHENOMENA + DATA What does the practice want to sense?Each row traces one practice's path: from curiosity → phenomena → hardware → software → work.The cascade is not a pipeline. It is a question: what does my practice want to know about the world, and what can transduce that?IR camera arrays + motion sensors ↓ Isadora — software they built themselves ↓ Real-time video, sound, and environment that respond to and shape the dancerTroika RanchMark Coniglio + Dawn StoppielloWhat does it mean for a dancer's body to generate the world the performance inhabits? Can the performer simultaneously cause and be caused by the environment?Movement → body position, velocity, gesture in spaceInfrared camera tracking → continuous positional + gestural data streams in real timeCamera + motion capture ↓ Custom visualization software (OSU ACCAD + The Forsythe Company) ↓ 89 interactive data objects — animations, scores, tools built from movementSynchronous Objects Archive SiteSynchronous Objects for One Flat Thing, reproducedChoreographic thinking doesn't disappear when the dance ends. Can movement organize things other than bodies? What other forms can choreographic structure take?Dance performance → motion tracking → relational + structural dataCuing patterns, spatial alignments, timing relationships extracted from a recorded piece of choreography
https://synchronousobjects.osu.edu
https://www.darrenwoodlandjr.com/?pgid=m7trkt3a-f47806de-2398-45e1-a3f4-d65148a5ca70
https://troikaranch.orgDIY handheld controllers + breath mouthpiece sensor + smartphone ↓ Pure Data + custom OSC routing ↓ Full live looping, synthesis, and arrangement — performed anywhere, no infrastructure neededOnyx Ashanti: This is beatjazz | TED Talk
https://www.ted.com/talks/onyx_ashanti_this_is_beatjazzbeatjazzThe Black body as a fully sovereign instrument. Full-spectrum musical autonomy — composition, performance, improvisation — all in and from the body. No stage, no studio, no separation between thinking and sounding.Hand position + breath + full-body movement → continuous gesture + breath dataThe body IS the instrument and the interface — not a metaphor but literally. Every movement is a performance decision.Learning to See Series (2017-) – Memo AktenLive video → real-time pixel data from a webcamBut the data the model actually uses is its training set — tens of thousands of images of natural phenomena. The webcam is the trigger. The dataset is the lens.Webcam → GPU compute ↓ Custom deep learning — trained only on natural phenomena (ocean, fire, clouds, aurora) ↓ Live video of hands and objects rendered in real time as whatever the model was trained to recognizeLearning to See (2017–)A neural network can only see through the filter of what it has already seen. What does that tell us about all seeing — human or machine? Perception is never a window. It's always a worldview.Can You See Me Now? | Location Based Game | Blast TheoryCan You See Me Now? (2001)Urban space as game board. Being seen, or not, as the actual stakes. What happens when players on the internet and runners in a physical city occupy and threaten each other in the same space?Physical location + network presence → GPS coordinates, player proximity, connection statusBeing caught = your GPS position and a runner's GPS position intersect. Presence is literally data. Absence is too.GPS receivers (worn by street runners) + handheld computers + walkie-talkies + networked server ↓ Custom real-time game engine + live mapping (Mixed Reality Lab, Nottingham) ↓ Mixed-reality chase: online players as avatars; runners as live GPS dots in the city
https://www.blasttheory.co.uk/projects/can-you-see-me-now/
https://www.memo.tv/works/learning-to-see/🟠 Movement / Dance / Interactive 🟣 Afrofuturist / Black Practice 🟡 Sound / Music 🔵 Computer Vision / ML-Visual 🟢 Biometric / Body 🔴 Instructor PracticeGeorge Lewis "Voyager" LIVE at the Bang on a Can Marathon 5/3/20 - YouTube
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncy4_FHX3JcLive instrumental performance → MIDI: note, velocity, timing, pitch, density dataThe data is musical behavior — not just notes but phrasing, energy, direction, momentum. The machine listens to all of it.Any MIDI instrument (trombone, saxophone, piano) ↓ Voyager — custom Lisp-based AI improvisation system (built at STEIM, Amsterdam) ↓ Virtual improvising orchestra: responds to the player AND generates independentlyVoyager (1987–)What would it mean for a machine to improvise in a Black musical tradition. Not mimicking it, but thinking with it? Can software carry cultural memory and agency?HKW | The Disappearance of Music: George Lewis: Timelike Weave | Voyager
https://archiv.hkw.de/en/programm/projekte/2020/das_verschwinden_der_musik/programm_verschwinden_der_musik/video_george_lewis_timelike_weave_voyager.php

item.title: Hardware Clarifications — Thinking Toward Sensors
item.description:
You may have heard the terms Stemma QT and Qwiic and Grove in lecture and wondered if they're different systems you need to choose between. They aren’t, really. There are some subtle differences between them, besides name, but they are types of either 3 prong or 4 prong connectors.Stemma QT (Adafruit) and Qwiic (SparkFun) are two brand names for the same electrical standard: a 4-pin JST-SH connector running I2C communication at 3.3V. The physical connector is identical. The electrical protocol is (nearly) identical. A Stemma QT cable plugs into a Qwiic board and vice versa, witt little to no modification needed.
Here is a working definition for this course:A sensor is anything that transduces a physical phenomenon into data your system can process.That definition is deliberately broad. It includes: An accelerometer/IMU that reads movement, orientation, and vibration A capacitive touch sensor that reads electrical conductance at discrete points A microphone that reads acoustic pressure over time A webcam that reads light as a 2D pixel grid at some frame rate A Kinect or depth camera that reads spatial distance and skeletal pose A GSR (galvanic skin response) sensor that reads electrodermal conductance as a proxy for physiological arousal A piezoelectric disc that reads mechanical deformation (pressure, impact, vibration) A GPS module that reads position in space relative to satellites A light sensor or color sensor that reads photon flux at various wavelengths A flex sensor that reads bend angle as changing resistance A game controller that reads button states, thumbstick positions, and rumble signals Notice that microphone, webcam, and Kinect are in that list. They are sensors too! What about computer vision — does it count? If you're using a webcam with software like MediaPipe, Wekinator, or OpenPose to extract gesture, pose, or facial landmarks, you're running a sensor and an interpretation layer on top of it. The sensor (webcam) reads raw pixel data. The model reads that data and outputs a higher-order description (hand position, skeletal angle, detected emotion). Both layers involve reduction and both layers are legitimate sites of creative and critical inquiry. The question to ask is: what does the model's interpretation assume about bodies, movement, and legibility? Who was the training data? Whose gesture gets read cleanly, and whose doesn't? An early pain point, as we have discovered together, is in approaching physical computing for the first time by starting with the sensor. So lets work backwards to the sensors starting with the thinking and curiosity!Working in this order will help keep your practice in the driver's seat. The sensor becomes an epistemic tool you've chosen for a reason.If your practice is drawn to movement, gesture, dance, or the body in space: → You're probably interested in orientation, acceleration, or spatial position data → Consider: IMU/accelerometer/gyroscope (Stemma QT options: LSM6DS3, LSM9DS1, BNO055), depth camera (Kinect, Intel RealSense), MediaPipe pose estimation via webcam
If your practice is drawn to touch, contact, material surfaces, textile, or skin: → You're probably interested in discrete contact events, pressure, or capacitance data → Consider: MPR121 capacitive touch (Stemma QT), FSR (force-sensitive resistors, any), piezoelectric transducers, velostat/conductive fabric
If your practice is drawn to sound, voice, sonic environment, acoustic space: → You're probably interested in amplitude, frequency content, onset events, or spectral shape → Consider: electret microphone + breakout, MEMS microphone (Stemma QT: PDM microphone), field recorders into audio analysis software, FFT in Max/MSP or TouchDesigner
If your practice is drawn to proximity, presence, or environmental sensing: → You're probably interested in distance, occupancy, or ambient conditions (temperature, light, humidity) → Consider: VL53L1X time-of-flight (Stemma QT), APDS-9960 proximity + color (Stemma QT), PIR motion sensor, thermal camera (AMG8833 grid-eye, Stemma QT)
If your practice is drawn to biological states (stress, arousal, breath, heartbeat): → You're probably interested in physiological signals as data (GSR, pulse, respiration, heat rate) → Consider: GSR sensor + voltage divider, MAX30102 pulse oximeter (Stemma QT), piezo on chest or wrist for breath/heartbeat, stretch sensor
Not an exhaustive list of pathways, but it is a start!Before we discuss specific hardware purchases or setups, answer these questions. Write them in your Critical Technical Journal if you’d like, or bring them as notes to discuss in class or in a message to me (the instructor). 1. What is your practice thinking about right now? Not what you want to make — what is your practice interested in? What questions, materials, bodies, phenomena, histories, or tensions keep pulling your attention? 2. What are you curious about in terms of physical phenomena? Movement? Contact? Sound? Environmental change? Biological states? Something else? More than one thing is fine. 3. What kinds of data would let you work with those phenomena? Try to be specific. Not "sensor data," but what kind of data? A stream of numbers? Threshold events (on/off)? A spatial map? A frequency spectrum? 4. Make a list. Based on your answers above, write a rough list of the types of data you think you need. Don't worry yet about whether a sensor exists for it. Just name what you want to know about the physical world. Once you have that list, we can map it to available sensors, identify what's accessible via Stemma QT / Qwiic, and figure out a reasonable path for your practice project.If you need to purchase sensors:
Adafruit (adafruit.com): primary source for Stemma QT ecosystem. Use the "Stemma QT" filter in their sensors category.
SparkFun (sparkfun.com): Qwiic ecosystem, fully compatible. Digikey / Mouser: for bulk or harder-to-find parts; more intimidating but comprehensive. Check the BB Lear site under /Resources/Shopping for Sensors/ for more useful info!If cost is a barrier, talk to the instructor before purchasing anything.

item.title: Hardware and Software Inventory
item.description:
"The digital system is material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." — Magnusson, Sonic Writing You could read this note as a checklist of tools we might be using this term. But given what we've spent W01A and W01B establishing that tools are epistemic, that instruments condition what can be thought, that amplification is always also reduction. Well, we can't rightly do that with a straight face, can we?Instead, consider this an epistemic inventory. For each element of the course toolkit, we'll be asking: what does this tool make possible, what does it foreclose, and why did we choose it?The physical-digital entanglement at the center of this course runs through a specific signal chain (maybe not this specifically, but something similar):Body / Material World ↓ MPR121 Sensor (capacitive touch) ↓ Adafruit QT Py RP2040 (microcontroller) ↓ CircuitPython (embedded code) ↓ OSC / UDP (protocol over Wi-Fi) ↓ TouchDesigner / Max/MSP / Ableton (host software) ↓ Sound, Image, Data Output Each arrow in this chain is a transformation. Each of those transformations amplifies something and also reduces something else. The QT Py RP2040 is a small microcontroller board built around the Raspberry Pi RP2040 chip. It runs CircuitPython a version of Python designed for embedded systems with limited memory and no operating system. Or it can also run Arduino or PlatformIO both versions of C++ for embedded systems. Why this board, epistemically?The QT Py is small enough to embed in an object, a garment, or a physical installation. We couldn’t do that with a desktop PC. So, this changes the relationship between the body and the computation. The computation moves toward the body rather than the body moving toward the computation. This also presents a design decision with consequences for what kind of physical-digital entanglement is possible.It also has explicit constraints: limited memory, no file system (without an SD card), no display, no persistent storage across power cycles. These are enabling constraints. They push us toward thinking about computation as a real-time process happening in a physical context, not a processing pipeline running on a workstation, rendered, then presented.Ihde's modalities here: In typical use, the microcontroller operates in a hermeneutic relation, meaning it produces data (sensor readings) that you then interpret in software. But as your fluency develops, it can shift toward an embodiment relation, where the hardware/body interface recedes and you're thinking directly in terms of interaction rather than data.The MPR121 detects electrical conductance at 12 separate electrode points. When a conductive object (a finger, a body part, water, conductive thread, foil, fruit, etc.) comes near or touches an electrode, the sensor registers a change in capacitance.Epistemic specifics:The MPR121 models the world as twelve discrete contact points with threshold values. It does not model pressure, velocity, texture, or gesture in any richer sense. This is a fairly substantial reduction, but also a generative constraint.Why 12? A speculative aside on hardware and tonality The MPR121's 12-electrode architecture is almost certainly a pragmatic engineering choice. 12 is a highly composite number, divisible by 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12 — which makes it a natural Schelling point in design: enough channels for most multi-touch applications, manageable over I2C, and culturally unremarkable. We already organise time in 12s (months, hours (non-24)), commerce in 12s (dozens, gross), and space in 12s (inches to the foot). All this to say, the number doesn't need music theory to justify itself. But the coincidence is worth sitting with, I think: 12 also happens to map cleanly onto the chromatic scale of Western 12-tone equal temperament. A person who assigns one pitch per electrode isn't fighting the hardware. They'd working with a latent affordance the chip happens to carry. Whether that affordance was designed or accidental doesn't change the fact that it's there, and that it quietly favors a particular musical cosmology over others. The epistemic question it opens: what would a 19-electrode sensor do to your compositional assumptions? What practices would suddenly feel natural, and whose tuning systems, microtonal, spectral, non-Western, would feel less like workarounds? What this reduction enables: you have to build gestural richness out of combination, sequencing, timing, and creative use of what "electrode" means materially. The sensor touching a piece of copper tape embedded in a textile or paper is not the same experience as touching a pad on a breakout board, even if the the electrical signal may be identical.The sensor does not care about the materiality of what it touches. That indifference is the limitation. Making that indifference expressive is the research-creation challenge.The Zoom H5 is a portable, mid-range field recorder. Four inputs (two XLR combo jacks, plus the built-in X/Y capsule pair), 24-32bit/96kHz recording, small enough to carry anywhere.Epistemic framing: The H5 models the world as microphone placements and headroom. Unlike software recording, field recording asks you to solve problems in space and time before you can solve them in software. You can't EQ a bad room placement (kinda). The recorder forces decisions about where you are and where the sound is in a way that a software sampler does not.The H5 is also a tool for practice-based research: documentation, listening, locating yourself in a sonic environment. Used as a research tool (not just a production tool), it is a way of attending to a space before you decide what to make there.CircuitPython is Python stripped down for embedded environments. The key constraint: no concurrency, no threads, single-threaded event loop. Your code runs top to bottom, repeatedly, in a tight main loop.Epistemic consequence: You cannot think about this system the way you think about desktop software. There is no background thread listening for events while the foreground does something else. Everything is sequential. This forces particular models of time, interaction, and performance. Actually, one that is closer to how musical performance works (step by step, no stopping) than how most software development works.The loop structure also makes the code's relationship to time explicit. The latency between sensing and responding is determined by how much work you do in each loop iteration. You feel computation as time.OSC is a protocol originally designed for real-time communication between musical instruments and software. It uses the UDP networking protocol, which means messages are sent in discrete packets that can arrive out of order or not at all. It is a protocol that prioritizes low latency over guaranteed delivery.Epistemic framing: OSC messages have a specific structure: an address pattern (like /sensor/touch/1) and typed arguments. This structure makes the musical/physical origin of the data visible in the data itself. Unlike MIDI, which was designed around keyboard-and-note-number logic, OSC is relatively free, the address namespace is whatever you define.The UDP choice (vs. TCP) is itself an argument about what matters: latency matters more than reliability. For real-time physical interaction, a dropped packet is usually less harmful than a 50ms delay. This is a design philosophy embedded in the computation and protocol.TouchDesigner is a node-based visual programming environment developed by Derivative, used widely for real-time visual performance, interactive installations, and physical computing. It receives OSC messages (among may other protocols like DMX, MIDI, etc.), processes them in a dataflow graph, and routes the results to visual, audio, or other outputs.Epistemic specifics:TouchDesigner models the world as a cooking system: operators (nodes) either cook (update their output) or don't, based on whether their inputs have changed. This is a specific model of reactive computation, and it is one that is very well suited for real-time visual work and less natural for sequential or text-based logic.The node-based paradigm also has an epistemological consequence: your decisions are made visible as connections. You can see the shape of your logic. This is different from writing code in an IDE, where the structure of your reasoning is embedded in and enabled by syntax. The defaults matter here (returning to Magnusson): the built-in operators in TouchDesigner assume certain things about color, resolution, framerate, and timing that reflect the tool's origins in VVVV and cinema-influenced real-time graphics. When you use those defaults without questioning them, you're (perhaps subconsciously) making an implicit argument about what your work should look like.Max/MSP (and its twin PureData) are the older cousins of TouchDesigner. They are node-based environments with deeper roots in algorithmic musical composition and signal processing. Where TouchDesigner is GPU-native and optimized for visual output, Max is CPU-native and optimized for audio, MIDI, and raw numerical data.Why both? The choice between TouchDesigner and Max is not always a purely technical one. Often times, it is partly a question of disciplinary genealogy. TouchDesigner comes from the VJ / visual performance world; Max comes from the electroacoustic music world. They carry different assumptions about what a "performance" is, what "real-time" means, and what relationship between software and body is natural.Using both is an opportunity to feel those differences in your body as you work and to make that felt for anyone interacting with your work.Here is the exercise this note is preparing you for:Do your own epistemic inventory. Pick tool(s) you already use in your practice, any tool(s) really, not necessarily the ones listed here. For each one: What does it amplify? (What becomes easy, visible, measurable?) What does it reduce? (What disappears, becomes invisible, gets rounded off?) What world does it assume exists? (What is the implicit model of activity, interaction, body, material that its design encodes?) Who designed those assumptions, and for what context? This exercise is the foundation of one of your ASN 2 (Critical Technical Journal). Signal chain — the full sequence of transformations from physical world to digital output; each link is a reduction/amplification pair OSC (Open Sound Control) — a real-time messaging protocol that allows physical sensors and software to communicate; address-based, free-form namespace Capacitive touch — detection of electrical conductance changes; models touch as threshold-crossing events at discrete electrode points Cooking system — TouchDesigner's model of reactive computation; operators update only when inputs change Default assumptions — the inherited worldviews encoded in software's standard settings and built-in abstractions The hardware described above is the course's core signal chain — but it is not a prescription for yours. Before choosing sensors or purchasing hardware, work through your own practice first.
See → Hardware Clarifications — Thinking Toward Sensors for a framework on how to move from practice thinking to sensor selection, a clarification on Stemma QT vs Qwiic, and the prompt to complete before our next hardware conversation.For CircuitPython + MPR121 + OSC → TouchDesigner:
Adafruit CircuitPython documentation
MPR121 CircuitPython library
TouchDesigner OSC In CHOP documentation
MicroOSC library for CircuitPython
Additional Adafruit CircuitPython libraries

item.title: DIGM 553 Syllabus — Spring 2026
item.description: Spring 2026 | 3.0 credits | GraduateLink to Course Syllabus PDF In this hands-on lab, students experiment with emerging tools and techniques, applying their creative vision to produce innovative digital media projects. This course encourages risk-taking and exploration, helping students develop unique projects that push the boundaries of digital art and design. Develop experimental digital media projects through a research-creation methodology that integrates critical inquiry, technical exploration, and creative production as co-constitutive practices. Critically interrogate digital tools as non-neutral agents that encode worldviews and actively structure the boundaries of creative practice. Recognize and articulate the entanglement of practitioner, tool, and material in the creative process. Design and iterate enabling constraints that guide the creative process without predetermining outcomes. Articulate the theoretical and conceptual stakes of experimental media work through written, spoken, and performative modes of rendering research public. Collaborate with peers through techniques of relation that foreground process, care, and collective becoming. Manning, E. & Massumi, B. (2014). Thought in the Act. Minnesota Press. Magnusson, T. (2019). "Epistemic Tools." In Sonic Writing. Bloomsbury. Agre, P. (1997). "Toward a Critical Technical Practice." In Computation and Human Experience. Cambridge. Loveless, N. (2019). "Haraway's Dog." In How to Make Art at the End of the World. Duke. Camus, A. & Vinck, D. (2019). "Unfolding Digital Materiality." In Digitalsts. Routledge. item.title: Epistemic Tools Introduction
item.description:
"Instruments have a life of their own. They do not merely follow theory; often they determine theory, because instruments determine what is possible, and what is possible determines to a large extent what can be thought." — Hankins & Silverman, quoted in Magnusson If W01Aestablished research-creation as the methodological orientation of this course, This section (W01B) establishes the epistemic status of the tools you work with.These two moves are connected: if making is already a mode of thinking, then the instrument you make with is already shaping the kinds of thought that are possible.This is what Magnusson, following Hankins & Silverman and Don Ihde, means by epistemic tools: instruments are not passive, nor neutral. Instruments (artistic, musical, scientific, or otherwise) act as active participants in the construction of knowledge. The choice of what instrument to use is also not neutral. It conditions what questions you can ask, what results you can produce, and, eventually, what can be considered beautiful, interesting, or true.For us, this puts our tool choices in a new light. Choosing TouchDesigner over Processing, Max/MSP over SuperCollider, a capacitive sensor over a camera are all epistemological decisions as much as they are technical ones.Don Ihde identified four phenomenological modalities of instrument-use. We will look at the three most prominent ways that instruments mediate between the body and the world:You act through the instrument, which extends your body or amplifies your senses. The instrument recedes into the background (the hidden 4th relation - Background Relations). You experience through and with technology, not at a technology. A well-practiced keyboard player doesn't think about the keys; they think about the music. The keys are an extension of the hand.The instrument produces data that you must interpret. A spectrograph, a heat map, an oscilloscope reading. The instrument mediates reality by translating it into a representation via abstractions, but that representation requires interpretive work to become knowledge.The instrument becomes something you engage with for its own sake, as a “quasi-other”, a presence with its own agency. Virtual reality headsets, interactive installations, or a generative system that responds to you all produce this kind of relation.Important These modalities should not be considered exclusive categories. Think of them more as tendencies. Any given practice involves mixtures and oscillations between them. And they are not value-neutral: each modality shapes what you notice, what you miss, and what you expect the instrument to do for you. One of Don Ihde's most directly practical insight: every instrument involves amplification-reduction transformations. It amplifies certain features of the world and reduces others. And there is no exception to this.One important question to always ask of a tool, technology, or model is: “What is gained and what is lost when I apply it?” A microphone (through a purely physical model/definition) amplifies pressure-wave events in a certain frequency ranges (based on it circuit design and construction) and reduces everything else. A MIDI controller amplifies discrete pitch/velocity events and reduces continuous, gestural sound. A capacitive touch sensor amplifies conductivity at specific points and reduces everything that isn't electrical contact. The danger is not that [tools/technologies/models/definitions] reduce. All of them do to some extent. The danger is forgetting that they do. When the reduction becomes invisible, the thing not being captured disappears from your thinking entirely.Magnusson on software: Musical software encodes inherited defaults: equal-tempered tuning, temporal quantization, note-based event models. But they aren’t musical “facts” or “truths” and they seldom capture the full range of musical expression. What they are contingent historical choices that have been naturalized through adoption (sometimes forced) and repeated use in which what was reduced has faded away. They have become what Latour (and Bowker & Star) call black boxes. A black box is an object or system whose internal workings have become invisible through repeated use. Latour: "objects establish themselves as black boxes through repeated use and in the process their origins disappear." Bowker and Star extend this: "the more naturalized the object becomes, the more unquestioning the relationship of the community to it; the more invisible the contingent and historical circumstances of its birth, the more it sinks into the community's routinely forgotten memory." Take note on what this means for practice: the tools you're most fluent with are the most dangerous. Fluency produces blindness. The instrument you've used for years is the instrument whose assumptions you've most thoroughly absorbed into your practice without noticing. Critical technical Practice (CTP) connection: This is why what Agre describes as the "split identity" matters. One foot in craft, one foot in critique. The craft foot needs fluency. The critique foot needs to keep opening the black boxes that fluency keeps closing.Philip Agre's phrase points to a specific version of “computational imperialism”: computers "aim to reinvent virtually every other site of practice in its own image." They are built from representational models and abstractions of the activities they will be used to perform. However, in doing so, But they also restructure those activities, fundamentally. Example A digital audio workstation (DAW) doesn't just record and edit audio. It restructures the practice of making music around the concept of a timeline, discrete regions, channels, effects chains, automation curves, etc… This perpetuates a model of music-making built by engineers with particular assumptions about what music is. A computer, then, does not simply have an instrumental use in a given site of practice; the computer is frequently about that site in its very design.This is why Agre says that technical people often experience phenomenological texts as "sounding like mysticism." The mismatch in philosophy and understanding exists because the computer's representational model and the phenomenologist's model of experience are genuinely incommensurable. You can't translate one into the other because they aren't the same kind of thing. Agre's solution: stop translating, start learning on their (meaning models and practice of phenomenological experiences) own terms.Thor Magnusson in ‘‘Sonic Writing” spins a particular historical framing of a driving problem this way: Western philosophy has long separated techne (making, craft, technique) from episteme (knowledge, theory, science). Instruments of art were not instruments of knowledge; skill was not wisdom.In more modern theory and practice, this separation is now being productively challenged: by cognitive science (embodied cognition, enactivism) by STS (Science and Technology Studies) by research-creation methodology by practitioners in new interfaces for musical expression, interactive art, and critical making. IN doing so, our instruments become epistemic, fusing instrument with composition, as in the works of Gordon Mumma, David Tudor, and other practitioners and disciplines. The digital system is, as Magnusson puts it, "material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." All three registers are active all at once.Three questions to hold as you work through this course:What does your tool amplify? What aspects of your practice does it make easier to see, hear, measure, or manipulate? What does your tool reduce? What is systematically missing from what your tool captures? What can't it represent How has the above shaped what you've been making? Who designed the magnification-reduction? The defaults in your software were chosen by someone with specific assumptions. What were those assumptions, and whose experience of the world did they take as universally applicable? Epistemic tool — an instrument that is a knowledge-making artifact; tools determine what is possible and thus what can be thought Embodiment / hermeneutic / alterity relations — Ihde's three phenomenological modalities of instrument-world relationship Amplification-reduction — every tool amplifies certain features and reduces others; no tool is neutral (Ihde) Black box — a naturalized object whose internal contingency has become invisible through repeated use (Latour, Bowker & Star) Computational imperialism — the tendency of computing to reinvent every site of practice in its own representational image (Agre) Techne / episteme — the historically-separated domains of craft-knowledge and theoretical-knowledge, now being rejoined

item.title: Research-Creation as Method
item.description:
"Making would already be thinking-in-action, and conceptualization a practice in its own right." — Manning & Massumi, Thought in the Act Most of what we call "research" and most of what we call "creative practice" assume they are separate, sequential, activities. Research produces knowledge. Then, practice produces work. The knowledge informs the work. The work illustrates the knowledge. This is the typical “institutional model” of knowledge production. It is also the model we're going to spend the rest of this course systematically inhabiting and turning.Research-creation, as described by the authors Manning & Massumi is an activity that occurs at what they call the prebifurcation point : the point just before research and creation diverge into the institutional structures that evaluate them by separate criteria. At that point, making and thinking are not distinct acts. They are two registers of the same act, happening simultaneously.The theme of Week 01 is "Practice Immanent Critique." Here's what that phrase means from the ground up.An immanent critique does not stand outside a system to pass judgment. Instead, it works from inside. Id does so in order to inhabit the structure, understand its logic from within, and then find the pressure points where it might be turned. Manning & Massumi's definition:"An immanent critique engages with new processes more than new products, from a constructivist angle. It seeks to energize new modes of activity, already in germ, that seem to offer a potential to escape or overspill ready-made channelings into the dominant value system. The strategy of immanent critique is to inhabit one's complicity and make it turn — in the sense in which butter 'turns' to curd."Notice what this requires: inhabiting complicity. You are not exempt from the system you critique. You work from within it, on its tools, in its institutions, using its grants and its grades. Immanent critique means doing that while turning it, not waiting until you're free of it to begin this form of practice.So, let’s analyze this from our shared perspective. For this course: We are working at a university. We use tools (TouchDesigner, Max/MSP, Ableton, Python) that carry embedded worldviews. We receive grades. All of this is our complicity. Immanent critique is the method by which we make that complicity productive rather than just reproductive.Manning & Massumi acknowledge a tension: the institutional framing of research-creation — especially in the context of digital media and media studies — pushes it toward "formatting artistic activity for more directly economic forms of delivery to stakeholders." Digital media works often get funded in part because they "employ the same technological platforms as the increasingly computerized economy."For us, this is a friction of our practice (and a contradiction that is not easily resolved). Our work is to neither ignore this friction nor be paralyzed by it. Instead we should treat it as what Agre would call a hassle: a recurring friction that is itself data about the structure of the field.The danger Manning & Massumi identify: research-creation "settles into a communication model revolving around the delivery of results." The goal instead is what they call "an interpenetration of processes rather than a communication of products."What does that mean in practice? When you work on a project in this course, you are not primarily building something that will be assessed. You are practicing something. Developing a relationship to your tools, your materials, and your questions. The artifact becomes secondary, it is the record of that practice, not the point of it.These are technically different acts. Framing is setting up a structure: here are the rules, here are the constraints, here is the question, go. Conditioning is bringing co-causes into interaction such that something emerges that neither cause alone would produce. "Conditioning consists in bringing co-causes into interaction, such that the participation yields something different from either acting alone… Emergent process, dedicated to the singular occurrence of the new, agitates inventively in an open field. Programmed organization, on the other hand, functions predictably in a bounded frame and lends itself to reproduction."In this class, we are going to try to condition rather than frame. We should strive to set up initial conditions; not attempt to predetermine outcomes.The concept that connects it all: enabling constraints.An enabling constraint is positive in its dynamic effect even though it may be limiting in its form. The classic example: gravity is a constraint on dance, but it enables the jump. Without gravity to push against, there is no arc, no lift, no landing. The jump is a collaboration between the dancer and gravity — two co-causes whose interaction produces something neither does alone."In our experience, unconstrained interaction rarely yields worthwhile effects."This applies directly to the hardware and software in this course. The MPR121 sensor constrains what counts as input. CircuitPython constrains what you can compute on the microcontroller. OSC protocol constrains the format of the data. These are not obstacles — they are the material conditions out of which something emerges. The question is not how to eliminate constraints but how to turn them from limitative to enabling.Manning & Massumi introduce the concept of techniques of relation: "devices for catalyzing and modulating interaction" that comprise "a domain of practice in their own right." Techniques of relation are are structural: they shape how things interact, how processes co-evolve, how different elements of a practice can be brought into productive contact. They operate in two modes: Techniques that set up initial conditions — propitious starting points for emergence Techniques that modulate an event as it moves through its phases — improvised steering without predetermined destination A key property: "Techniques as we understand them do not depend exclusively on the content of the practices but move across their respective processes at the site of their potential multiplication." A technique is transferable. It can move from sound to movement to code to pedagogy.Assignment connection: Part of your ASN 2 (Critical Technical Journal) practice is to identify the techniques of relation already operating in your practice in order to begin consciously designing new ones.If every practice is already a mode of thought, what is your current practice thinking?Manning & Massumi open Thought in the Act with: "Every practice is a mode of thought, already in the act. To dance: a thinking in movement. To paint: a thinking through color. To perceive in the everyday: a thinking of the world's varied ways of affording itself."So for us: To program is a thinking in what? To route audio signals is a thinking in what? To touch a capacitive sensor is a thinking in what? To capture field recordings is a thinking in what? Right now, these are more rhetorical questions, but your first journal entries will begin to answer them, literally. Research-creation — activity at the prebifurcation point where making and thinking are co-constitutive, not sequential Immanent critique — inhabiting complicity and making it turn; critique from inside, not outside Enabling constraint — a limitation that, through interaction with other forces, generates emergence rather than just restriction Conditioning — bringing co-causes into interaction toward open, emergent outcomes (vs. framing toward predetermined ones) Techniques of relation — devices for catalyzing and modulating interaction; transferable across practices Manning + Massumi — Thought in the Act (Propositions 0–3, pp. 83–97)

(Im)material Potluck — Preparation
item.description:
Due: Week 02 - Bring your contribution to class. This is part of ASN 1: Potluck + Speculative Proposal.The (Im)material Potluck is a collective opening ritual for the course. Each student brings one thing — physical or immaterial — to contribute to a shared conversation about material, tools, and practice. It is as much a show-and-tell as it is an opening proposition.Consider the object you bring is an argument. It says something about your practice, your research, your questions. Your job is to be able to articulate what argument yours is making. Your contribution can be physical or immaterial, hence (im)material. What it cannot be is arbitrary. It should be something with stakes for your own work.Physical examples: A material you keep returning to (fabric, copper tape, wood, clay, wire) A piece of hardware that has shaped how you think (a sensor, a circuit board, a connector, an old device) An object from your research environment (something from a site you've been working in) A tool that frustrates you in productive ways Immaterial examples: A dataset, protocol, or schema you work with A sound or sound file (something you've recorded or that recurs in your practice) A constraint or rule you've imposed on yourself An image, a diagram, a piece of notation A system or process (something that has no single physical form) If your contribution is immaterial, come ready to share it on screen/speakers or describe it precisely. Vagueness is not the same as immateriality.For each contribution, you'll have a few minutes to speak (~5min). Prepare to address:1. Why this thing? Not its origin story — the practical reason it has stakes in your work. What does this object or material make possible in your practice that other things don't? What does working with it feel like, and what does that feeling tell you? 2. What does it open? What questions does it raise that you can't yet answer? What does it put into contact with other things in your work? Where does it lead?3. What is it thinking? Manning & Massumi: "Every practice is a mode of thought, already in the act." Objects and materials are part of practices: they aren't passive. What mode of thought is already active in the thing you're bringing? What does it do to the practice it's part of — not just what you do with it, but what it does to you? You don't need fully formed answers. You need to have asked the questions and be willing to sit with them in the room.The reading assigned this week is useful preparation for how to think about your object before you bring it. A few entry points:Manning & Massumi: They distinguish between framing (setting up a structure in advance) and conditioning (bringing co-causes into interaction to produce emergence). Is your object a frame or a condition? What does it enable that you didn't design in advance? There is no size or format requirement. One thing is enough. If it's fragile, pack accordingly. If it's large, photograph it and bring the photo plus a fragment. If it's truly immaterial and screen-sharing is difficult, prepare a 30-second verbal description precise enough that the room can hold it. You will not be graded on the quality of the object, only on the specificity and honesty of how you speak about it (plus your reflection post on it as well! ).

item.title: Final Presentation
item.description: Weight: 20%Render your work public. This 12–15 minute presentation (Week 11) should expose the formative forces of the project.This is not "here is what I made." It is: here is how the encounter with tools/materials changed the inquiry. The process is part of the work. The presentation must make the invisible labor, decisions, pivots, and transformations visible. Entry point — What was your driving curiosity? What was your dog? The matter-network — What tools/materials were you entangled with? Impasses and pivots — What resisted? What did that reveal? The work — Demonstration/documentation of the project Formative forces — How did the encounter with tools/materials change the inquiry? Open questions — What does this work open that it doesn't answer? Recorded presentation with demonstration. 12–15 minutes.Documentation (slides, video, or equivalent) submitted to Blackboard. Revised Speculative Proposal also due this week.

item.title: Critical Technical Journal
item.description: Weight: 25%Throughout the course, maintain a journal documenting your making process and reflexive critique. This journal captures all smaller post-class deliverables. Technical Documentation — What did you make, what did you try, what broke? Epistemic Interrogation — What is your tool thinking? What does your process assume? Entanglement Mapping — How are you, your tools, and your materials mutually transforming each other? Covers course opening through proposal. Includes: Journal Entry 0: Potluck reflection (Week 2) Journal Entry 1: Epistemic Tool Audit (Week 3) — choose one software + one hardware tool; map what each knows, assumes, and forecloses Speculative Proposal (see ASN 1) Deep making phase. Includes: Journal Entry 2: First Impasse Report (Week 5) — what has resisted; what the impasse reveals Mid-term presentation materials Final development phase. Includes: Journal Entry 3: Process Seed Reflection (Week 8) — what emerged from the seed exchange Final project documentation The journal can take many forms: physical notebook, blog, digital whiteboard, PDF, video diary, etc. Format can be negotiated with the instructor. Installments submitted as PDF to Blackboard at three specific checkpoints.Depth of engagement, documentation quality, honest tracking of failure/pivot.

item.title: Structured Dialogue + Participation
item.description: Weight: 10%Participation in two formal review sessions (Weeks 6 & 9) and the mid-term presentation (Week 7). This grade also encompasses larger class engagement throughout.Critique sessions utilize the Six Thinking Hats format to focus on activating potential rather than rendering judgment: White Hat — Facts and data: what is actually here? Red Hat — Intuition and feeling: what does this project make you feel? Black Hat — Caution: what are the risks or gaps? Yellow Hat — Optimism: what is the potential? Green Hat — Creativity: what else could this become? Blue Hat — Process: what questions should we be asking? Generosity of engagement, quality of critical application, collective thinking.

item.title: Experimental Media Project
item.description: Weight: 35%Develop an original digital media project that demonstrates thinking-in-action. Projects are encouraged to utilize physical computing hardware entangled with software environments. Evaluated on the rigor of the path taken, not just final polish.This is not a "make a cool thing" assignment. It is a research-creation project: the making process is the research. The project should demonstrate how your encounter with tools and materials transformed your initial inquiry. The project should show evidence of risk, impasse, pivot, and transformation.Projects should engage with at least one physical computing element (Adafruit QT Py RP2040, MPR121 touch sensor, or equivalent) entangled with a software environment (TouchDesigner, Max/MSP, p5.js, Pure Data, Unity, or equivalent).Early explorations feeding into the Speculative Proposal.Mid-term presentation focuses on what isn't working and what that reveals. Not a polish presentation — an honest reckoning with impasse.Final build + documentation uploaded to Blackboard. Documentation should include: project description, process narrative, technical documentation, and reflection on how the project changed from proposal to completion.Creative risk, conceptual-material integration, technical engagement, research-creation methodology.

item.title: Potluck + Speculative Proposal
item.description: Weight: 10%This bundled assessment comprises the early foundational exercises of the course. It includes your contribution to the Week 2 (Im)material Potluck and your formal Speculative Proposal (living document).Bring one (im)material thing to contribute to the collective. It can be physical (a texture, an object, a circuit board component) or immaterial (a dataset, a protocol, a sound, a constraint). Be prepared to explain why this thing and what it opens.The Proposal articulates: (a) Your driving curiosity — your "dog" (Loveless/Haraway): the specific, situated relation that animates your inquiry (b) Selected enabling constraints — at least 3 constraints designed to guide without predetermining (c) The matter-network — a map of the tools/materials/environments you are working with (d) Epistemic Positioning Statement — a paragraph on how your tools encode a worldview and how you are working with/against that A revised version of the Speculative Proposal reflecting how the project has transformed. What changed and why?Conceptual rigor, specificity of constraints, tool analysis, processual transformation.PDF uploaded to Blackboard. Due: Week 4 (initial) + Week 10 (revised).
